(Sūrat al-Naml is Makkan, and it has ninety-three or ninety-four verses.)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ta. Sin.﴾ It is read with tafkhim (emphatic pronunciation), and it has also been read with imalah (inclination). What is said about it is the same as what was said about its counterparts among the noble opening letters (al-fawatih). On the assumption that it is the name of the surah, and this is the most evident and best-known view, its position is nominative, as the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: this is "Ta. Sin," that is, it is named by it. Pointing to it (with the demonstrative) before it is mentioned has had its rationale explained at the opening of Sūrat Yūnus and elsewhere. Making it nominative as the subject, with what follows as its predicate, is weak for the reason mentioned there.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the surah itself, since it is the one that has been marked out by the mention of its name, not to its verses, because it is not explicitly mentioned; its being attached to verses would be inconsistent with its being attached to the Qur'an, as will come. The sense of distance carried by the demonstrative, despite the recency of reference to what is pointed at, is to signal the elevated rank of the surah in excellence and nobility. Its position is nominative as a subject, and its predicate is ﴿the verses of the Qur'an﴾. The sentence is a resumed clause that confirms what the naming conveyed about the distinguished standing of what is named. "The Qur'an" is either a designation for the whole, or for the entire collection revealed at the time the surah was revealed, as stated at the opening of the Book (al-Fatihah). That is: this surah is among the verses of the Qur'an, which is known for its lofty status, that is, a part of it, translated and independent under a particular name.

﴿And a Book﴾ that is of great importance, ﴿clear﴾, manifesting what is within its contents of judgments and rulings, and the states of the Hereafter, among which are reward and punishment, or the path of rectitude and error, or distinguishing between truth and falsehood, the lawful and the unlawful, or evidently miraculous, taking "mubin" as from abana in the sense of baana (to be evident). He has magnified its exalted rank by combining in it the attribute of being Qur'an, which indicates that it is unique in its kind and distinguished from others by its miraculous composition, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿a Qur'an in Arabic, without any crookedness﴾. The attribute of being a Book, which indicates that it comprises the attributes of perfection of the divine books, so that it is as though it were all of them, is also mentioned. He placed the first attribute first here, in view of the priority of the state of being Qur'an over the state of being a Book, and reversed it in Sūrat al-Hijr, in view of the aspect mentioned there. What is said, that the Book is the Preserved Tablet and its clarity is that what is to occur has been inscribed in it, so it makes it clear to those who look into it, is not supported by the attachment of verses to it, since there is no established basis for it containing verses, nor by describing it as guidance and good tidings, since these are in terms of its being made clear; so it is necessary to consider them in relation to people, among whom are the believers, not to those who look into it. It has also been read as "wa-kitabu" in the nominative, by deleting the annexed term and placing the annexed-to term in its position, meaning: and the verses of a clear Book.

Guidance and good news for the believers. [This is] in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "the verses," with both words being verbal nouns (maṣdar) used in the sense of active participles for emphasis, as if they were themselves the guidance and the good news, the governing element being the sense of indication (al-ishārah), meaning: guiding and bringing good news. Or they may be in the nominative, as substitutes (badal) for "the verses," or as two further predicates for "those," or as predicates of an omitted subject. The meaning of its guiding them, while they are guided, is that it increases them in guidance, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice.﴾ As for the meaning of its giving them good news, it is evident, for it gives them good news of mercy from Allah, His good pleasure, and gardens in which they will have lasting bliss.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 3:

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Who establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾, are a descriptive attribute praising them. Singling out these two is because they are the twin companions of faith (qarinatā al-iman) and the two pillars (qutrā) of the bodily and financial acts of worship, and they entail all the other righteous deeds.

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And they, of the Hereafter, they are certain﴾, form a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tiradiyya), as if it were said: "These who believe and do righteous deeds are the ones who are certain of the Hereafter with true certainty, not others, because bearing the hardships of worship is out of fear of punishment and hope for reward." Or it is a continuation of the relative clause, with the waw being a circumstantial waw (waw al-hal). Or it is a conjunction linking it to the first relative clause, and the change in its wording serves to indicate the strength and steadfastness of their certainty and that they are unique in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾: an explanation of the states of the disbelievers after the explanation of the states of the believers. That is, they do not believe in it (the Hereafter) and in what it contains of reward for righteous deeds and punishment for evil deeds, as the Qur'an declares.

﴿We made their deeds appealing to them﴾: the ugly deeds, in that We made them desired by the natural disposition and loved by the self, as indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Fire is surrounded by desires." Or (it means) the good deeds, by making clear their goodness in themselves in the present and their leading to various kinds of benefits in the future, and the attribution of them to them is in regard to their being commanded with them and obligated to them.

﴿So they wander blindly﴾: they are bewildered and hesitate, continually and persistently. Thus, with their preoccupation with them and their immersion in them, without considering what follows them of benefit or harm; or, in error and turning away from them. The "fa" (so) according to the first (interpretation) indicates the ordering of the effect upon the cause, and according to the second indicates the ordering of the opposite of the effect upon the cause, as in your saying: "I admonished him, but he did not heed admonition." It contains an indication of the completeness of their obstinacy, their arrogance, and their reversal of affairs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 5:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those previously mentioned. It is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is the relative clause (al-mawsul) following it, i.e., "those characterized by disbelief and blindness" ﴿who will have an evil punishment﴾, i.e., in this world, such as being killed and taken captive on the day of Badr. (p-273)

﴿And in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾, i.e., the most extreme of people in loss, due to the forfeiting of reward and the incurring of punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 6:

﴿And indeed, you are being given the Qur'an⟩ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), introduced after the explanation of some aspects of the Noble Qur'an as a preparation for the stories that follow it. Its opening with the two emphatic particles (harfa al-taʾkid) serves to display the utmost concern for its content; that is, you are receiving it by way of being given it and being instructed in it (al-talqiyah wa-al-talqin).

﴿from the Presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾. That is: what a Wise One and what an All-Knowing One! In magnifying these two attributes there is a magnification of the status of the Qur'an, and an explicit statement of the high rank of the Prophet ﷺ in knowing it and comprehending what it contains of sublime and subtle matters. For whoever receives knowledge and wisdom from such an All-Wise, All-Knowing One becomes a distinguished figure in the solidity of knowledge (ʿilm) and wisdom (hikmah), and in combining the two, with knowledge entering into wisdom because of the generality of knowledge, and because wisdom indicates the perfection of action. It is also to indicate that the knowledge in the Qur'an is of two kinds: some of it is wisdom, such as the doctrines (ʿaqaʾid) and the legal rulings (sharaʾi'), and some of it is not so, such as the stories (qisas) and the unseen reports (akhbar al-ghaybiyyah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 7:

The phrase "Wa qawluhu ta'ala" (And His saying, exalted is He) — ﴿Idh qala Musa li-ahlihi﴾ (When Musa said to his family) — is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi) of a hidden verb addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), commanding him to recite a portion of the Qur'an that comes to him (ﷺ) from His Presence, exalted and majestic is He, as an affirmation (taqrir) of what precedes it and a confirmation (tahqiq) of it. That is: "Mention to them the time when he (upon him be blessings and peace) said to his family in the valley of Tuwa, when the darkness of the night had enveloped them and he had struck (the flint) and its tinder had produced a spark, and a fire appeared to him from the side of the Mount."

﴿Inni anastu naran, sa-atikum minha bi-khabar﴾ (Indeed I perceived a fire; I will bring you from it news) — that is, about the condition of the road, for they had lost their way. The sin (in sa-atikum) indicates a degree of distance in the journey and the emphasis of the promise. As for the plural, if it is correct that he (upon him be blessings and peace) was accompanied only by his wife, then he referred to her with the word "family" (ahl) by way of euphemism; or it is for magnification, as an intensification of consolation.

﴿Aw atikum bi-shihabin qabas﴾ (Or I will bring you a brand of fire, a burning ember) — with both words nunated (tanwin), on the basis that the second is a substitute (badal) for the first, or an attribute (sifah) of it, because it carries the meaning of maqbus (taken from a fire), that is: "with a torch of fire taken (maqbusah), that is, taken from its source." It was also read with the idafah (construct). On both readings, the intended aim is to specify the desired object, which is the qabas (ember) that combines the benefit of light and the benefit of warmth, because among fire there is that which is not a qabas, such as a live coal. Both of these benefits he (upon him be blessings and peace) hoped to obtain, by way of conjecture, as is made clear by the expression of hope (tarajji) in (Surat Ta-Ha). The alternation (tardid) serves to indicate that if he did not obtain both, he would not be deprived of one of them, based on the apparent state of affairs and trust in the custom of God Most High, for He, exalted is He, scarcely gathers two deprivations upon His servant.

﴿La'allakum tastalun﴾ (That perhaps you may warm yourselves) — hoping that you may warm yourselves by it. And "al-sila'" (ṣilāʾ): a great fire.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 27, verse 8:**

﴿So when he came to it, he was called﴾ from the side of the mount (al-Tur): ﴿"Blessed is"﴾. Its meaning is: "Blessed is," where "an" (that) is explanatory (mufassira), explaining the sense of speech contained in the call. Or it is "that Blessed is," where "an" is verbal (masdariyya), with the preposition omitted from it according to the established rule. It is also said that it is light (mukhaffafa) from the heavy form (thaqila), and there is no harm in the absence of compensation by "la," "qad," "sin," or "sawfa," because supplication (du'a') differs from other speech in many rulings.

﴿"Whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it"﴾: that is, whoever is in the place of the fire, which is the blessed ground mentioned in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿"He was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed ground"﴾ (p-274), and whoever is around its location. It was also read: "Blessed is the land and whoever is around it." The apparent meaning is general, to everyone in that valley and around it, from the land of al-Sham, which is marked by blessings, because it is the place where the prophets were sent, peace be upon them, and where they are gathered, alive and dead. This is especially so for that ground where God, exalted is He, spoke to Musa. It is also said that what is intended is Musa and the angels present. The opening of the address with this is a good tiding that a great religious matter has been decreed for him, whose blessings will spread through the regions of al-Sham. This is His speaking to him, exalted is He, his being made a prophet, and the manifestation of miracles at his hand, peace be upon him.

﴿"And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds"﴾: this is an expression of wonder to Musa, peace be upon him, at that, and an announcement that it is what He wills and brings into being, the Lord of the worlds. It is a reminder that what occurs is among the sublime matters and great affairs, and among the rulings of His nurturing of the worlds, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 9:

﴿O Musa, indeed it is I, Allah﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to explain the effects of the blessing mentioned. The pronoun (damir) may refer to the matter of the situation (li-al-sha'n), with "I am Allah" being an explanatory sentence (jumla mufassira) for it; or it may refer back to the speaker, with "I" being its predicate (khabar) and "Allah" an appositive (bayan) for it.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾ are two attributes of Allah, exalted is He, which prepare the ground for the miracles intended to be manifested through His hand (yad), that is: I am the Strong, the Capable, over what the imaginings cannot reach of great matters, among which is the matter of the staff and the hand. And everything I do is done with far-reaching wisdom (hikma baligha) and firm governance (tadbir rasin).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 10:**

﴿And throw down your staff﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "Blessed is" (būrika), strung together with it in the same thread as the explanation of the call (tafsīr al-nidāʾ). That is: it was called out that "blessed is..." and that "throw down your staff," according to what His saying, Exalted is He, expresses: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾, by repeating the interpretive particle (ḥarf al-tafsīr), just as you say: "I wrote to him that perform ḥajj, and that perform ʿumrah, and if you wish, that perform ḥajj and ʿumrah."

The fāʾ in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So when he saw it moving﴾ is eloquent (faṣīḥah), disclosing a sentence that has been omitted, relying on its being evident and indicating the swiftness with which its content occurred, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So when they saw him, they magnified him﴾, after His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Go forth to them﴾. It is as if it was said: "So he threw it, and it turned into a serpent moving swiftly, and he saw it; so when he saw it moving quickly and convulsing..."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿as though it were a jinn﴾, meaning: a light serpent, swift in movement, is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), either from the object of "saw" in the manner of "moving" as has been indicated, or from the pronoun in "moving" according to the method of interpenetration (tadākhul). It has been read "jaʾnun" according to the dialect of one who strives in fleeing from the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn).

﴿and he turned to flee﴾ out of fear, ﴿and did not look back﴾, meaning: he did not return upon his heels, from ʿaqqaba (the fighter): when he turned back after fleeing. He was seized by terror only because he thought that this was for a matter intended for him, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿O Moses, do not fear﴾, meaning: from other than Me, trusting in Me, or absolutely, due to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾, for it indicates the negation of fear from them absolutely, but not at all times; rather at the time they are being revealed to, as at the time of address, for at that time they are wholly absorbed in contemplating the affairs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and no fear of anyone at all occurs to their minds. As for the rest of the time, they are the most fearful of people of Him, glorified is He. Or it means: there is no evil consequence for them with Me, so that they should fear from Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 11:

(p-275) ﴿Except for one who has done wrong and then substituted good after evil; indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), by which he corrects what might occur to the mind of fear being negated for all of them, given that some of them may have committed a minor sin (saghirah) of the kind that it is permissible for the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, to commit. For even if something of that sort proceeded from them, they immediately did what nullifies it, and thereby they deserve forgiveness and mercy from God the Exalted. He intended by this an allusion to what occurred from Moses, upon him be prayer and peace, in striking the Copt and seeking forgiveness, and calling it a wrong (zulm), in accordance with his (ﷺ) saying: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me,﴾ and so He forgave him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 12:

﴿And put your hand into your bosom﴾ because it was a woolen garment (mudarra'a) with no sleeve. It was also said: the jayb (bosom) is the shirt, because it is cut open (yuja, i.e., cut).

﴿It will come out white, without harm﴾ meaning a defect such as leprosy or the like. ﴿Among nine signs﴾ within their number or along with them, on the basis that the nine are: the splitting of the sea (al-falq), the flood (al-tufan), the locusts (al-jarad), the lice (al-qummal), the frogs (al-dafadi'), the blood (al-dam), the obliteration (al-tamsa), the drought in their deserts (al-jadb fi bawadihim), and the shortage in their fields (al-nuqsan fi mazari'ihim). For one who counts the staff and the hand among the nine, the last two may be counted as one, and the splitting is not counted among them, because it was not sent with him to Pharaoh. Or the phrase ﴿Go to Pharaoh and his people with nine signs﴾ is taken as a new sentence about the sending, so that it is connected to it: ﴿to Pharaoh and his people﴾. On the first two readings, it is connected to a verb such as mab'uthan (sent) or mursalan (dispatched).

﴿Indeed, they were a people of defiant transgression﴾ a reason for the sending, meaning: those who went beyond the limits in disbelief and aggression.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 13:

﴿So when Our signs came to them﴾ and appeared at the hand of Musa (Moses), ﴿visible﴾, meaning clear. Mubsirah is an active participle (ism fa'il) used in the sense of a passive participle, which indicates that, because of their extreme clarity and brightness, it is as if they could see themselves, if they were the kind of thing that sees. Or it means "possessing insight," in that they guide, whereas the blind are not guided, let alone able to guide others. Or it means "giving sight to everyone who looks at them and reflects upon them." It was also read "mabsarah" (مَبْصَرَةً), meaning a place where much insight occurs.

﴿They said, "This is manifest magic."﴾ Its being magic is clear.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 14:**

﴿And they denied them⦆ — that is, they denied them (the signs). ﴿And their souls were certain of them⦆ — the waw here is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), meaning: while their souls had certainty of them, that is, their souls knew them with certain knowledge (ʿilman yaqiniyyan).

﴿Wrongfully⦆ — that is, against the signs, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿because they used to wrong Our signs⦆. Indeed they wronged them in the worst way, in that they brought them down from their elevated rank and called them magic. It has also been said: "wrongfully" against themselves, but this is not the correct view.

﴿And arrogantly⦆ — that is, out of pride in refusing to believe in them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who denied Our signs and were arrogant towards them⦆. The two words (ẓulman and ʿuluwwan) are in the accusative either as a reason for (ʿilla for) ﴿they denied them⦆, or as a circumstantial accusative (ḥal) referring to their subject, meaning: they denied them while wronging them and being arrogant towards them.

﴿So see how was the end of the corrupters⦆ — from the drowning, in the awesome manner that is a lesson for the worlds. He did not mention it explicitly as a warning that it is exposed to every observer, well known among everyone present and absent.

(p-276) ﴿And We certainly gave knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾. This is a fresh statement, brought in to confirm what preceded it: that the Prophet (ﷺ) receives the Qur'an from One who is Wise and All-Knowing. Their story, peace be upon them, is part of the noble Qur'an, which the Prophet (ﷺ) received from Him, Exalted is He, just as the story of Musa, peace be upon him. The opening with an oath (qasam) serves to show the utmost care in affirming its content. That is: We gave each of them a portion of knowledge fitting to him, from the knowledge of laws and rulings and other things specific to each of them, such as the craft of making coats of mail and the speech of the birds; or [it means] a lofty and mighty knowledge.

﴿And they both said﴾, i.e., each of them said, in gratitude for the knowledge given to him: ﴿All praise is for Allah, who has favoured us﴾ with what He gave us of knowledge ﴿over many of His believing servants﴾. Although each one's statement would be "He has favoured me," the plural "us" is used when relating it, for brevity. The relating of multiple statements, whether they were uttered by the speaker or by someone else, in a comprehensive expression that covers all of them is not uncommon. Of the first kind is His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾, which has been discussed in (Surat Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun). By this the excellence of the conjunction with "wa" (and) becomes evident, since what is immediately understood from a conjunction with "fa" (then) is that each one's praise is consequent upon the giving of what each was given, not merely upon the giving of what he himself was given. It has also been said that the conjunction with "wa" indicates that what they said was part of what was produced in them by the bestowal of knowledge and some of its obligations; so that was left implicit and the praise was then conjoined to it, as if it were said: "And We certainly gave them knowledge, so they acted upon it and We taught it to them, and they recognised the due right of this blessing," then ﴿"And they both said: All praise is for Allah..."﴾ the verse. So reflect. The "many" over whom they were favoured are those who were not given knowledge like theirs; and it has been said: those who were not given any knowledge. But the specifying of "many" by "of the believers" argues against this, for their being entirely devoid of knowledge is impossible. In singling out the majority for mention there is a hint that some are favoured over them. In this is the clearest proof of the excellence of knowledge and the nobility of its people, in that they gave thanks for knowledge and made it the basis of excellence, and did not regard above it the kingship they were given, which no one else was given. It is also an exhortation to scholars to praise Allah, Exalted is He, for what He has granted them of His bounty, to be humble, and to believe that although they are favoured over many, many are favoured over them, for "over every possessor of knowledge is One All-Knowing." How well said was the Commander of the Faithful, Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Every person is more knowledgeable than Umar."

﴿And Solomon inherited David﴾: that is, prophethood and knowledge, or kingship, in that he took his place in it, to the exclusion of the rest of his sons, who numbered nineteen.

﴿And he said﴾: to make known the blessing of God Most High, to highlight it, and to call people to believe by mentioning the dazzling miracles he was given.

﴿O people, we have been taught the speech (mantiq) of the birds and have been given of everything﴾. In common usage, mantiq (speech, language) is any utterance by which what is in the mind is expressed, whether single or compound. It may also be applied to any sound by which something is conveyed, whether single or composed, meaningful or meaningless. One says: "the dove spoke" (nataqat al-hamamah). Every species of birds has sounds by which they make themselves understood. What Solomon, peace be upon him, was taught of the speech of the birds is what some of them understand from others of their meanings and purposes. It is related that he passed by a nightingale (bulbul) in a tree, moving its head and inclining its tail, and he said to his companions: "Do you know what it is saying?" They said: "God and His Prophet know best." He said: (p-277) "It says: when I eat half a date, then the world is of no account (fa-ala al-dunya al-'afa')." A ring-dove (fakhitah) cried out, and he reported that it was saying: "Would that creation had not been created." A peacock (tawus) cried out, and he said: "It says: as you judge, so you will be judged." A hoopoe (hudhud) cried out, and he said: "It says: seek forgiveness from God, O sinners." A tayTawa (a small bird) cried out, and he said: "It says: every living thing dies, and everything new will wear out." A swallow (khuttaf) cried out, and he said: "It says: send forward some good, you will find it." A turtledove (qamari) cried out, and he reported that it was saying: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." A vulture (rakhmah) cried out, and he said: "It says: Glory be to my Lord, the Most High, filling His heaven and His earth." He said: the kite (hidaah) says: "Everything perishes except God." The sand grouse (qata) says: "Whoever keeps silent is safe." The parrot (babbaghaa) says: "Woe to him whose concern is the world." The rooster (dik) says: "Remember God, O heedless ones." The eagle (nisr) says: "O son of Adam, live as you wish, your end is death." The owl (uqab) says: "In distance from people there is intimacy." The frog (difda') says: "Glory be to my Lord, the Holy." By his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, "we have been taught" and "we have been given," with the nun known as the nun of the one obeyed (nun al-wahid al-muta') [the royal plural], he describes his condition and attribute, namely that he was a king who was obeyed, but not out of tyranny or arrogance, rather as a preparation for what he desired from them of good obedience and submission to him in his commands and prohibitions, since he was resolved to lead them. By his saying "of everything," he means the abundance of what he was given, as one says: "So-and-so is sought by everyone and knows everything," meaning the multitude of those who seek him and the abundance of his knowledge. Similar to this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "Everything that concerns him of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter." Muqatil said: "He means prophethood, kingship, the subjugation of the jinn, mankind, the devils and the wind."

﴿Indeed, this﴾: a reference to what has been mentioned of teaching and giving ﴿is truly the grace﴾ and the favour from God Most High ﴿manifest﴾: the clear one that is hidden from no one. Or: this grace that he was given is truly the manifest grace. He, peace be upon him, said it by way of thanks and praise, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: ﴿I am the master of the sons of Adam, and without boasting﴾; that is, I say this statement in thanks, not in boasting. Perhaps, peace be upon him, by his words he meant to make the people ready for holy war, for informing them that everything has been given to him, among which are the instruments of war and the means of campaigning, indicates that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 17:

The meaning of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And his hosts were gathered together for Solomon﴾, that is, his armies were assembled for him, ﴿from among the jinn and mankind and the birds﴾, through the direct involvement of those addressed, for they were the leaders of his kingdom and the great men of his state, from both the two species (the jinn and mankind) and others. The generalization of "people" (al-nas) to all of them is by way of taghlib (predominance of one term over another). The mention of the jinn before mankind in the exposition is to hasten the announcement of the perfection of his dominion's strength and the might of his authority from the very beginning, since the jinn are a rebellious group, a transgressing and insolent tribe, far from being gathered and subjugated.

﴿So they were being marshalled﴾, that is, the first of them were held back for the last of them, meaning the vanguard of the army were halted until the rear caught up with them, so that they would be assembled and none of them would lag behind; and this is due to the enormous multitude. It is also possible that this was for the arrangement of the ranks, as is customary in armies. In it there is an indication of the perfection of their haste in marching, and the specific mention of holding back the first of them without mentioning driving on the last of them, even though catching up also occurs by that means, is because the last of them are not able to do what the first of them are able to do of swift march. This applies when their march is not by the wind's conveyance through the air.

It is related that his army, peace be upon him, was a hundred farsakhs in extent, comprising a hundred parts: twenty-five for the jinn, twenty-five for mankind, twenty-five for the birds, and twenty-five for the wild beasts. He, peace be upon him, had a thousand tents of glass set upon wood, in which were three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines. The jinn had woven for him a carpet of gold and silk, a farsakh by a farsakh, and his pulpit, which was of gold, would be placed in its middle, and he would sit upon it, and around him were six hundred thousand chairs of gold and silver. The prophets, peace be upon them, would sit upon the golden chairs, and the scholars upon the silver chairs, and around them the people, and around the people the jinn and the devils. The birds would shade him with their wings so that the sun would not fall upon him, and the gentle east wind would lift the carpet and carry him a month's journey.

It is also related that he would command the violent wind to carry him and command the gentle breeze to move him; so God Exalted revealed to him while he was travelling between heaven and earth: "I have increased your kingdom; no one speaks a word but that the wind casts it into your hearing." It is recounted that he passed by a ploughman and said: "Indeed the family of David has been given a mighty kingdom," and the wind cast it into his ear; so he descended and walked to the ploughman and said: "I only came to you so that you would not wish for what you cannot attain." Then he said: "Truly, one single glorification that God Exalted accepts is better than what the family of David has been given."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 18:

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾ "Hatta (until) is the particle with which speech begins, and yet it is also an end-point (ghayah) for what precedes it, like the hatta in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when Our command came and the oven gushed forth, We said: Load into it...﴾ and so on to the end of the verse. Here it marks the end-point of what is indicated by His words: ﴿so they were marshalled﴾ (from the march), as if it were said: 'So they marched until, when they came upon...' and so on. The valley of the ants (Wadi al-Naml): a valley in al-Sham abounding in ants, according to what Muqatil, may Allah be pleased with him, said; and in al-Ta'if according to what Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, said. It was also said: it is a valley inhabited by jinn, and the ants are their mounts. The verb is connected to it by the word 'ala ('upon') either because their coming was from above, or because the meaning of coming upon it is traversing it, from the saying 'ata 'ala al-shay' when he exhausted it and reached its end. Perhaps they intended to descend at the end of the valley, for then the creatures of the earth would fear them, not while they were travelling in the air.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿A certain ant said﴾ are the answer to 'idha (when). As if, when she saw them heading towards the valley, she fled from them and cried out a cry by which those ants near her were alerted to her purpose, so they followed her in fleeing. This was likened to addressing rational beings and advising them, so they were given the same treatment: she was made the speaker, and the rest of the ants were made the addressees, where it is said: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾. Yet it is not impossible that Allah, exalted is He, should create speech in her and understanding and comprehension in the rest of them. It was recited as "namlatun ya ayyuha al-namlu" with a damma on the mim, which is the original form, like al-rajul; and sukun on the mim is a lightening of it, like al-sab' for al-sabu'. It was also recited with a damma on the nun and the mim. It was said: she was a lame ant who walked limping, and she called out with what she said, and Sulayman, peace be upon him, heard her speech from three miles away. It was also said: her name was Takhiyah. It was recited: "maskanakum".

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Let not Sulayman and his hosts crush you﴾ are, in reality, a prohibition addressed to the ants against delaying their entry into their dwellings, although outwardly it is a prohibition addressed to him, peace be upon him, and to his hosts against crushing, like their saying: "I shall not let you see me here." So it is either a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) or a substitute (badal) for the command, like the words of one who said:

"I said to him: Depart, let me not see you staying with us..."

It has no answer, for the nun (of emphasis) does not enter it in ample usage. It was recited: "la yuhattimannakum" with the light nun, and it was recited: la yahattamannakum with fath and kasr on the ha', and its original form is la yahtatimannakum.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ are a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of yuhattimannakum, specifying the crushing as occurring in a state in which they are unaware of their location, such that if they perceived it they would not be crushed. She intended by this to make known that she has knowledge of the affairs of Sulayman and of all the prophets, peace be upon them, and of their being protected from injustice and harm. It was also said: it is a resumptive sentence, meaning that Sulayman understood what she said while the people (p-279) did not perceive it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 19:

﴿So he smiled, laughing, at her words﴾ (wonder at her caution and her perceiving how to arrange the welfare of herself and of her kind), and (joy) at the renown of his state and the state of his soldiers in the matter of piety and compassion among the classes of created beings, which are farthest from grasping such matters, and (delight) at what Allah the Exalted had bestowed upon him of perceiving her whisper and understanding her intent. It is related that she sensed the sound of the soldiers while not knowing that they were in the air, so Sulayman, peace be upon him, commanded the wind, and it stood still lest they be frightened, until they entered their dwellings.

﴿And he said: My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favor﴾ That is: make me restrain (aza'a) the thanks for Your blessing that is with me, hold it fast and bind it, such that it does not slip away from me, so that I am never separated from thanking You at all. It has also been read with a fatha on the ya' of "awzi'ni."

﴿which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents﴾ Their mention is included here to multiply the blessing, for bestowing favor upon them is a favor upon him, which calls for gratitude.

﴿and that I may do righteousness which You approve﴾ as a completion of gratitude and a perpetuation of the blessing. ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ among their company, into Paradise, which is the abode of the righteous.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 20:

﴿And he inspected the birds﴾. That is: he sought to know the condition of the birds, and did not see the hoopoe (al-hudhud) among them. ﴿So he said: "Why is it that I do not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾ It is as if he said at first: "Why do I not see him? Is it because something has concealed him, or for some other reason?" Then it became clear to him that he was absent, so he turned away from that and began to say: "Is he absent?"

﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will surely slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority.﴾

It was said: his punishment of the hoopoe consisted of plucking out its feathers and exposing it to the sun. It was also said: he would place it together with its opposite in a cage. It was also said: by separating it from its mate.

﴿Or I will surely slaughter him﴾ so that the others of its kind might take warning from him.

﴿Or he must bring me a clear authority﴾ meaning a proof that makes clear his excuse. The oath, in reality, is sworn upon one of the first two alternatives on the assumption that the third does not occur. It has also been recited as "la-ya'tiyannanni" with two nuns, the first of them vowelled with a fatha and doubled. It was said that when he, upon him be peace, finished building the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem's sanctuary), he prepared for the Hajj with his troops, arrived at the Haram, and remained there as long as he willed, sacrificing each day, throughout his stay, five thousand camels, five thousand cows and twenty thousand sheep. Then he resolved to set out for Yemen, and he departed from Makkah in the morning, heading for Suhayl, and reached Sana'a at midday, a journey of one month. He saw a beautiful land whose greenery pleased him, so he alighted to eat and pray, but he found no water. The hoopoe was his water-finder (qannaq), and it could see water beneath the earth as one sees water in a glass bottle. The devils would come and flay the ground as a hide is flayed, and extract the water. So he searched for it for that reason.

(p-280)When Sulayman (peace be upon him) descended there, the hoopoe (hudhud) circled overhead and saw another hoopoe perched, so it swooped down to it. It described to it the kingdom of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and all that had been subjected to him. Its companion told it of the kingdom of Bilqis, and that under her hand were twelve thousand commanders, each commander having a hundred thousand under his hand. The hoopoe then went with it to look, and did not return until after the afternoon prayer. This is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he stayed not long﴾, that is, for a not lengthy period. It was also read with a dammah on the kaf (fa-makatha ghayra ba'idin, with the kaf vowelled with a dammah).

It is mentioned that a breath of the sun fell upon the head of Sulayman (peace be upon him), so he looked and found the place of the hoopoe empty. He summoned the 'arif al-tayr (the chief overseer of the birds), who is the eagle (al-nasr), and asked him about it, but did not find its knowledge with him. Then he said to the sayyid al-tayr (the lord of the birds), who is the falcon (al-'uqab): "Bring it to me." So it rose up, looked, and saw the hoopoe approaching. It made for it, and the hoopoe adjured it by God, saying: "By the right of God who gave you strength and power over me, will you not have mercy on me?" So it let it go. The hoopoe said: "May your mother be bereaved of you! Indeed, the Prophet of God has sworn that he will surely punish you." It said: "Did he make an exception?" The eagle said: "Yes." The hoopoe said: "Or he will bring me a clear excuse." When it drew near to Sulayman (peace be upon him), it lowered its tail and wings, dragging them along the ground in humility before him. When it came close to him, Sulayman (peace be upon him) seized it by its head and drew it towards him. It said: "O Prophet of God, remember your standing before God, Exalted is He." Sulayman (peace be upon him) trembled and pardoned it. Then he questioned it, and it said: ﴿I have encompassed that which you have not encompassed﴾, that is, in knowledge and understanding, and it had comprehended it from all its aspects. It was also read as "uhittu" with the ta' of the verb assimilated into the ta' (idgham al-ta' fi al-ta'), both with and without emphatic articulation (ittibaq).

There is no doubt that by what it claimed, it did not mean encompassing those realities of knowledge and subtle insights whose knowing and encompassing are the duties of the people of knowledge and wisdom, since they depend upon firm knowledge and clear excellence. For it to assert such a thing for itself in the presence of the Prophet of God Sulayman (peace be upon him) would be an overstepping of its station and a transgression beyond the bounds of its rank. To negate it of him (peace be upon him) would be a sin upon a sin, requiring one to excuse him by saying that this was a revelation through the way of inspiration (al-ilham). Thus he (peace be upon him) would be confronted with it, despite what he had been given of the excellence of prophethood, wisdom, abundant knowledge, and encompassing many known things, as a trial for him (peace be upon him) in his knowledge, and as an admonition that among the lowest and weakest of God's creatures there may be one who encompasses in knowledge what another has not encompassed, so that his soul may regard it as small and his knowledge may appear small to him, and it would be a kindness to him in abandoning self-admiration (al-i'jab), which is the trial of scholars. Rather, it meant by this what is among the perceptible matters, for whose encompassing no virtue is counted and whose neglect is no deficiency, since their apprehension depends only upon mere sense perception, in which the intelligent and others are equal. It knew with certainty that he (peace be upon him) had not witnessed it nor heard its report from anyone else, so it expressed it by what was mentioned, in order to make his speech acceptable to him (peace be upon him), to encourage him to listen to its excuse, and to incline his heart towards accepting it, for the soul is more receptive to an excuse that announces a wondrous matter and more inclined to receive what it does not know.

Then it confirmed this with his words: ﴿And I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾, where it explained its vagueness to some extent, and it intended (peace be upon him) that it was engaged in performing an important service for him, since it described what it brought as al-naba' (the momentous news), which is a weighty report and a great matter, and described it with what it described. Otherwise, what had come from him (peace be upon him) in addition to what has been related of his praise and thanks, and his seeking of al-ii'za (the spur to gratitude), so that it would befit divine wisdom, would have been a warning from him (peace be upon him) against its neglect.

Saba' is declined (munsarif) on the basis that it is the name of a tribe (hayy) named after their greatest forefather, who is Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. They said: his name was 'Abd Shams, and he was given this epithet because he was the first to take captives (sabi). It was also read with a fatha on the hamza, not declined (ghayra munsarif), on the basis that it is the name of a tribe. Then the city of Ma'rib was named after Saba', and between them and Sana'a is a three-day journey. On this reading it is possible that the intended meaning is either the tribe or the city, whereas on the first reading the intended meaning is only the tribe, and nothing else.

Sulayman's (peace be upon him) not having knowledge of their news before the hoopoe informed him is not a strange matter that must have some wisdom prompting it, though it is impossible that God's acts be devoid of wisdoms and benefits. For though the distance between his (peace be upon him) station (p-281) and Ma'rib was short, the period between his descent there and the hoopoe's bringing of the report was also short. Yes, the hoopoe's being singled out for this, although the jinn are stronger than it, is based upon profound wisdoms that only the Knower of the Unseen (Allam al-Ghuyub) keeps to Himself.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 23:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the news he brought and detailing it after its summary. She is Bilqis, daughter of Shurahil ibn Malik ibn Rayyan. Her father was king of the whole land of Yemen. He inherited the kingship from forty fathers, and he had no child other than her. After him she prevailed over the kingship, and the community submitted to her. She and her people were Magians who worshipped the sun. The choice of "wajadtu" (I found) over "ra'aytu" (I saw) indicates, as has been pointed out, the announcement that he, in his absence, was about to serve him, peace be upon him, by presenting himself in the manner of one who inquires into her conditions and gets to know them, as though she were his quarry and his lost thing, so that he might present her to Solomon, peace be upon him. The pronoun in "tamlukuhum" refers to Saba', either as the name of a people, or to its people, understood from the mention of their city, as the name of it.

﴿And she has been given of everything﴾, that is: of the things that kings need.

﴿And she has a mighty throne﴾. It was said: it was thirty cubits by thirty in width and height, and it was said: eighty by eighty, of gold and silver, inlaid with jewels. Its supports were of red and green ruby, pearls and emerald, and upon it were seven chambers, on each chamber a locked door. The hoopoe's magnifying of her throne, despite what he had witnessed of Solomon's kingdom, is either relative to her condition, or relative to the thrones of kings like her, and it has been allowed that Solomon, peace be upon him, had one like it. In any case, his describing it in that way before him, peace be upon him, is because of what has passed of his, peace be upon him, encouraging him to listen to his account, and directing his, peace be upon him, resolve towards subjugating her.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 24:

Therefore He followed it with what the conquest of her (the queen's) kingdom required, because of her disbelief and the disbelief of her people, when she said: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾, meaning: they worship it, going beyond the worship of Allah the Exalted.

﴿And Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾, which are the worship of the sun and its like among the kinds of disbelief and sins, ﴿and so he averted them﴾ by that means ﴿from the path﴾, meaning: the path of truth and rightness. For the adornment of their deeds cannot be conceived without the straightening of the ways of their disbelief and misguidance, and it necessarily entails attributing crookedness to the way of truth.

﴿So they﴾ by that means ﴿do not find guidance﴾ to it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 25:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Not to prostrate to Allah﴾ is a *maf'ul lahu* (object of purpose), either governed by *al-sadd* (barring) or by *al-tazyin* (adorning), with the *lam* elided from it. That is: He barred them so that they would not prostrate to Him, the Exalted; or He adorned for them their deeds so that they would not prostrate. Or it is a *badal* (substitute) in its own position for "their deeds," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*), meaning: He adorned for them that they should not prostrate. It has also been said that it is in the position of the object of *layahtadun* (they are not guided), with the preposition dropped, and *la* is superfluous, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so that the People of the Book may know...﴾. The meaning is: they are not guided to prostrate to Him, the Exalted.

It was also read as *ala ya-smudu* (Ah, prostrate!) with *tanbih* (alerting), and the vocative and the one called are elided, meaning: *ala ya qawmu-smudu* (Ah, O people, prostrate!), as in the saying:

> Ah, O Salma, be well, O abode of Mayy, though worn by time

and its like. On this reading it may be a fresh statement (*isti'naf*) from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, or from Sulayman, peace be upon him. In that case one pauses at *la yahtadun* and it becomes a command to prostrate. On the earlier readings it is a censure for abandoning it. In every case, prostration is obligatory.

It was also read *halla* and *hala* with the two hamzas changed to *ha'*, and it was read *halla* *tasjudun* (you prostrate), meaning *ala tasjudun* (will you not prostrate), in the second-person address.

﴿Who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth﴾, that is: He makes manifest what is concealed and hidden in them, whatever it may be. The specification of this attribute for mention, in the context of showing that He alone deserves prostration, from among His other attributes which necessitate that, is because it is more firmly rooted in knowledge of Him and comprehensive awareness of His rulings through witnessing His effects, among which is what Allah, the Exalted, has placed in Him of the power to know water beneath the earth. By coupling His saying ﴿and He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ to *yukhriju* (He brings forth), He indicates that He, the Exalted, brings forth what is hidden in the human world just as He brings forth what is hidden in the greater world, because the intended meaning is that He manifests what you conceal of conditions and then recompenses you for them. The mention of *ma tu'linun* (what you disclose) is to broaden the scope of knowledge, or to alert to their equality in relation to divine knowledge.

It was read *ma yukhfuna wa ma yu'linun* (what they conceal and what they disclose) in the third-person form, without a shift in address. The bringing forth of what is hidden encompasses the shining of the stars and their appearance from their horizons after being hidden behind them, the sending down of rain, the growth of plants, and indeed *al-insha'* (origination), which is bringing what is in a thing potentially into actuality, and *al-ibda'* (innovation), which is bringing what is in possibility and non-existence into existence, and other of His unseen matters, Mighty and Majestic.

It was read *al-khab* with the hamza lightened by deletion, and it was read *al-khabba* with it lightened by substitution, and it was read: ﴿Not to prostrate to Allah, who brings forth the hidden from the heavens and the earth and knows your secret and what you disclose﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 26:

﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Lord of the Mighty Throne.﴾ He who is the first and greatest of the celestial bodies. It is also read "al-'Azīmu" (the Mighty) in the nominative case, as an attribute of the Lord. Know that what is related from the hoopoe, from his saying ﴿Who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth﴾ up to here, is not included under his saying ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾. Rather, it is from the knowledge and insights which he acquired from Sulayman (peace be upon him). He presented it as an explanation of his own condition and a demonstration of his steadfastness in the religion. All of this serves to direct the heart of Sulayman (peace and blessings be upon him) toward accepting his speech and to turn the reins of his resolve (peace be upon him) toward conquering her land and subjecting its rule.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 27:

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), coming as an answer to a question that arises from the reported speech of the hoopoe (hudhhud). It is as if it were said: "What did Sulayman, peace be upon him, do at that point?" So it is said: "He said: ﴿We shall see﴾," i.e., regarding what you have mentioned of looking (naẓar), in the sense of reflection (ta'ammul). The sīn (in sananẓuru) is for emphasis, meaning: we shall certainly learn by testing.

﴿Have you spoken the truth, or have you been one of the liars?﴾ The apparent expectation would have been "or have you lied," but the choice of the wording the noble text uses is to indicate that his lying in this matter necessitates his being counted among those marked with lying and firmly rooted in it. For the course of these fabricated statements, arranged in an elegant order that inclines the hearts of the listeners toward accepting them without their having any actual basis at all, is especially so in the presence of a prophet of great rank, from whom such a thing would hardly proceed except from one who has a firm foothold in falsehood and fabrication.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 28:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go with this letter of mine and cast it to them﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of the observation which he (peace be upon him) had promised. He (peace be upon him) said it after he had written his letter in that assembly, or after it. His (peace be upon him) singling out of the letter for delivery, rather than the rest of the strong jinn trustees under his dominion who are capable of acting and of discerning, was because of what he had observed in it of the signs of knowledge and wisdom and the soundness of insight (firasah), and so that no excuse whatsoever would remain for them.

﴿Then withdraw from them﴾, that is: move aside to a nearby place where you may conceal yourself, ﴿and observe﴾, that is: reflect and discern ﴿what they return﴾, that is: what some of them return to one another of speech. The plural of the pronouns is because the content of the noble letter is a call of all of them to Islam.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 29:

﴿She said﴾ i.e., after the hoopoe had gone off with the letter, thrown it to them, and withdrawn from them as he had been commanded. The mention of him was left out (ṭuwiya dhikruhu) to signal the extent of his haste in carrying out the service he had been ordered to perform, and to indicate that he needed no explicit mention because his role was so evident.

It is narrated that (upon him be peace) wrote his letter, sealed it with musk, stamped it with his signet ring, and gave it to the hoopoe. The hoopoe found her (the queen) asleep in her palace at Ma'rib. Whenever she slept, she would lock the doors and place the keys under her head. So he entered through a window (kuwwa), and the letter was dropped onto her chest while she lay on her back. It is also said that he pecked her, and she woke up startled. It is also said that he came to her while her commanders and troops were around her, and he hovered for a while as the people watched, until she lifted her head, and he dropped the letter onto her lap. She was literate, a writer, an Arab, from the lineage of Tubba' al-Himyari, as has passed. When she saw the signet, she trembled and submitted. At that point she said to the nobles of her people: ﴿O chiefs, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾. She described it as noble either because of the nobility of its content, or because it came from a noble king, or because it was sealed, or because of the strangeness of its matter and its reaching her by a way that was not customary.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 30:

﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman﴾. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), coming as a reply to an implied question, as if it had been said: "From whom is it, and what is its content?" So she said: "Indeed it is from Sulayman." "And indeed it" means: its content, or what is written in it, ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. In this there is an indication of the reason for her describing it as noble (karim).

It has also been read as "annahu" and "anahu" with a fatha, on the basis of the omission of the lam (hadhf al-lam), as if she were giving as the reason for its nobility that it is from Sulayman and that it begins with the name of Allah the Exalted. It has been said that it is in apposition (badal) to "kitab" (letter). It has also been read as "an min Sulayman" and "an bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim," with "an" being the explanatory "an" (al-mufassirah).

**"Do not exalt yourselves against me"** (ألا تَعْلُوا عَلَيَّ). Here "an" (أنْ) is explanatory (mufassirah), and "la" (لا) is prohibitive. That is, do not act arrogantly as the tyrannical kings do. It is also said that "an" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah nasibah) governing the verb, and "la" is negating, with its place in the nominative case, either because the clause is from the book, or as the predicate of an implied subject suited to the context, meaning: its content is that you should not exalt yourselves. Or it is in the accusative by removal of the governing preposition, meaning: "that you should not exalt yourselves against me." It is also recited as "an la taghluw" (أنْ لا تَغْلُوا) with a dotted ghayn (غين مُعْجَمَة), meaning: do not transgress your limits.

**"And come to me in submission"** (وَأْتُونِي مُسْلِمِينَ). That is, believers. It is also said: submitting. The first meaning is the more fitting to the station of the Prophet (ﷺ), since faith necessarily entails submission. It is related that the letter from the servant of God, Sulayman ibn Dawud, to Bilqis, queen of Saba', read: "Peace be upon him who follows the guidance. Now then, do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission." The letter does not command Islam before the establishment of proof for his messengership, such that it might be imagined to be a call to imitation (taqlid). Rather, delivering the letter to her in that condition is a manifest miracle, clearly indicating the messengership of the one who sent it.

(p-284)﴿She said﴾. The reporting of her words is repeated to signal the great care she took with what lies within its scope of her saying: ﴿O chiefs, give me your opinion (afatūnī) on my matter﴾. That is, answer me concerning my matter, which has distressed me, and whose essence I have mentioned to you. I expressed the answer by *fatwā* (a legal judgment or considered answer, the usual term for a response to difficult cases), to magnify the matter and to raise their standing, by indicating that they are able to resolve pressing difficulties.

And her saying: ﴿I would not decide a matter﴾, that is, of the affairs connected with the kingdom, ﴿until you witness it﴾, that is, except in your presence and in accordance with your opinions. This is an appeal to them and an attempt to win their hearts, so that they will not oppose her in opinion and management.

**They said**: This is a resumptive statement (istinaf) built upon a question arising from the narration of her words, as if it were said: "What did they say in reply to her?" So it was said: they said, **"We are possessors of strength"** in bodies, weapons and equipment, **"and possessors of mighty might"**, that is, valor, extreme courage and proven prowess in war.

**"And the command is yours"**, that is, it is entrusted to you, **"so consider what you will command."** We are obedient to you, so command us with your order and we will carry it out and follow your opinion. They meant: we are men of war, not men of counsel and consultation; the opinion and the management belong to you, so consider what you see, and we will be at your service.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 34:

When she sensed from them an inclination toward fighting and a deviation from the path of rectitude, she began to undermine their stance, which was founded on heedlessness of the matter of Sulayman, peace be upon him. This is her saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town﴾ of the towns, following the methods of warriors and combat, ﴿they corrupt it﴾ by destroying its buildings and wasting what it contains of wealth, ﴿and they make the honored of its people humble﴾ by killing, taking captive, expelling, and other kinds of humiliation and degradation.

﴿And thus do they do﴾ is an emphasis on what she described of their condition, by way of a concluding parenthetical digression (i'tiraDh tadhyili), and a confirmation of it, that this is their constant custom. It was also said: it is a confirmation of her words from God, may He be exalted, in the manner of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾ following His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Even if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted﴾.

**And indeed I am sending them a gift** (﴿وَإنِّي مُرْسِلَةٌ إلَيْهِمْ بِهَدِيَّةٍ﴾) is a restatement of her opinion after she had cast doubt on their views. She used the nominal sentence, which indicates constancy, and opened it with the emphatic particle *inna* (the particle of affirmation), to signal that she was resolved upon her opinion, that nothing would turn her from it and no inclination would make her waver. That is, "And indeed I am sending to them envoys with a great gift, **so I will see with what the envoys return** (﴿فَناظِرَةٌ بِمَ يَرْجِعُ المُرْسَلُونَ﴾), until I act according to what the situation requires."

It is reported that she sent five hundred boys dressed in the clothing of girls, with bracelets, armlets and earrings as their adornments, riding horses covered with brocade, whose bridles and saddles were of gold set with jewels; and five hundred girls on mounts, dressed as boys; and a thousand bricks of gold and silver; and a crown encrusted with pearls, tall rubies, musk and ambergris; and a casket containing a virgin pearl and a jasper stone with a crooked hole. She also sent a man of the noblest of her people, **al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr**, one of the people of judgment and intellect, and she said: "If he is a prophet, he will distinguish between the boys and the girls, will pierce the pearl with a straight hole, and will thread a string through the bead."

Then she said to al-Mundhir: "If he looks at you with an angry glance, then he is a king, so do not be alarmed by him. But if you see him with a gentle **shās** (a sidelong, sly glance), then he is a prophet." (p-285)

The hoopoe came and informed Sulayman, peace be upon him, of this. So he commanded the jinn, and they struck bricks of gold and silver and laid them out in an open courtyard before him, its length being seven **farsakhs** (parasangs). They placed around the courtyard a wall whose battlements were of gold and silver. He commanded that the finest of the animals of land and sea be brought, and they were tethered to the right and left of the courtyard, standing on the bricks. He also commanded that the children of the jinn, who were a great multitude, be stationed on the right and on the left. Then he sat upon his throne, with the chairs on either side of him, and the devils were arranged in rows stretching for farsakhs, the humans likewise in rows stretching for farsakhs, and the wild beasts, predators, birds and creeping creatures likewise.

When the people drew near and looked, they were astonished, and they saw the animals dunging upon the bricks. Their own souls then seemed small to them, and they threw away what they had brought with them. When they stood before him, he looked at them with a cheerful face and said: "What is behind you?" And he said: "Where is the casket?" Gabriel, peace be upon both of them, informed him of what was in it, so he said to them: "Indeed, in it is such and such." Then he commanded the termite, and it took a hair and passed through the pearl, and he made its provision in the tree. And a white worm took the thread in its mouth and passed through the jasper stone, and he made its provision in the fruits. He then called for water, and the girl would take water in her hand and put it in the other, then strike her face with it, while the boy, as he took it, would strike his face with it.

Then he rejected the gift, and that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when [the envoy] came to Solomon﴾, that is, the messenger, ﴿he said﴾, that is, addressing the messenger and the sender, giving precedence to the present over the absent. It was also said that he addressed the messenger and those with him, and this is supported by the reading "So when they came" (fa-lamma jaa'uu). The first view is preferable, because it contains greater emphasis on the denunciation and rebuke, and because it includes both of them, Bilqis and her people. The singular in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Return to them﴾, supports this.

﴿Will you aid me with wealth?﴾ This is a denunciation of their aiding him, peace be upon him, with wealth, despite his high rank and the vastness of his dominion, and a rebuke to them for it. The indefiniteness of "wealth" (mal) is for belittlement. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾, that is, than what you have seen of its signs, namely prophethood and a kingship beyond which there is no further end, ﴿is better than what He has given you﴾, that is, of wealth, of which what you have brought is part. Therefore I have no need of your gift, and it holds no weight with me. This is the reason for the denunciation. Perhaps he, peace be upon him, said these words to them, to the end, only after what had passed between him and them, of the story of the truth and other matters, as has been indicated, and not that he, peace be upon him, addressed them with these words the first time they came to him, as may be understood from the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: "So when he came..." etc. It has also been read as "atumiddunnanii" with assimilation, with one nun, with two nuns, and with the omission of the ya'.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Rather, you rejoice in your gift﴾ is a turning away from what was mentioned of the denunciation of aiding him with wealth, to a rebuke for their rejoicing in their gift which they had presented to him, peace be upon him, the rejoicing of pride, boasting and self-regard in it, as is indicated by what was mentioned of the story of the truth and the jaza'ah (the vessels), and the change of dress of the boys and the girls, and other things. The benefit of the turning away is to alert that aiding him, peace be upon him, with wealth is a reprehensible and ugly thing, and that counting that, while it has no worth in his sight, peace be upon him, is among the things over which competitors compete, is uglier, and the rebuke for it is more pointed. It was also said: the mudaf ilayhi (the genitive complement) is the one to whom the gift is given, and the meaning is: "Rather, you rejoice in what is presented to you, out of love for increase of wealth, because you know only the outward appearance of the life of this world."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 37:

﴿Return﴾. He used the singular pronoun here, after the plural pronouns of the five preceding instances, because the return is specific to the Messenger, while the general sense of the provision and the like applies to all. That is: "Return, O Messenger, ﴿to them﴾, that is, to Bilqis and her people. ﴿Then we will surely come to them﴾, that is, by Allah, we will surely come to them ﴿with armies they cannot withstand﴾, that is, they have no power to resist them and no ability to confront them." It has also been read as "bihim" (with them).

﴿And we will surely expel them﴾ is a conjunction with the answer of the oath, ﴿from it﴾, from Saba', ﴿humiliated﴾, that is, in a state of being humiliated after what they had been in of might and establishment. The use of the plural of paucity (adhillah) emphasizes their humiliation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will be debased﴾, that is, captives, abased, is another state, indicating that their expulsion will be by way of capture and not by way of exile. The answer of the oath did not occur because it was conditional on a condition that was omitted at the time of the narration, trusting in the indication of the situation, as if it were said: "Return to them, so let them come to you in submission; otherwise we will surely come to them," and so on.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 38:

﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ He (peace be upon him) said this when the arrival of Bilqis (the Queen of Sheba) to him (peace be upon him) drew near. It is narrated that when her envoys returned to her with what had been reported of the account of Sulayman (peace be upon him), she said: "By God, I know that this is not a king, and we have no power against him." She sent to Sulayman (peace be upon him): "I am coming to you with the nobles of my people, so that I may see what he commands and what he calls to of his religion." Then she announced her departure to Sulayman (peace be upon him), and she set out to him with twelve thousand qayl (chieftains or commanders), each of whom had thousands under him. It is also narrated that she gave an order, and her throne was placed in the innermost of seven enclosures, one within another, in the last of seven palaces that belonged to her. She locked the doors and appointed guards to protect it. Perhaps it was revealed to Sulayman (peace be upon him) that she had secured her throne, so he wished to show her some of the marvels that God, exalted is His dominion, had granted him by performing wonders through his hand, along with making her aware of the great power of God, exalted is He, and the soundness of His prophethood (peace be upon him), and to test her intellect by having her throne disguised, so that he could see whether she would recognize it or not. The restriction of the bringing of the throne by the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿before they come to me in submission﴾ is because that is more wondrous, more remarkable, and further from what happens ordinarily, and more indicative of the great power of God, exalted is He, and of the soundness of the prophethood of (the Prophet) (peace be upon him); and so that her testing and her being made aware of the marvels of miracles occur at the first of her arrival. It was also said: because if she came in submission, it would not be lawful for him to take her property without her consent.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 39:**

﴿He said, "A ʿifrīt (a powerful, wicked demon) from among the jinn"﴾: that is, a wicked rebel. ﴿from among the jinn﴾ explains it, since the term ʿifrīt is said of a wicked, defiant man who subdues his peers. His name was Dhakwān or Sakhr.

﴿"I will bring it to you"﴾: that is, her throne. ﴿"before you rise from your place"﴾: that is, from your seat for judgment. He used to sit until midday. The word "ātīka" (I will bring you) may be the active participle or the imperfect form. The participle is more fitting to the claim that he will certainly bring it, and it better matches the nominal clause coordinated with it, meaning: "I am definitely bringing it within that period."

﴿"And indeed I am strong enough for it"﴾: that is, for bringing it. ﴿"trustworthy"﴾: I will not carry its weight with difficulty, nor will I take any part of it or alter it.

﴿Qāla alladhī ʿindahu ʿilmun mina al-kitāb﴾ [He said, "One who had knowledge from the Book"]. It is separated from what precedes it to signal the difference between the two speakers and their two statements, and the difference between their abilities to bring the throne, which is of the utmost contrast. Or it is separated to remove the first speaker from the level of consideration. It is said that he was Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, the vizier of Sulaymān, peace be upon him. It is said that he was a man who had the Greatest Name of God (al-ism al-aʿẓam), which when invoked, He answers. It is said that he was al-Khiḍr, or Jibrīl, or an angel whom God, Mighty and Majestic, strengthened with it, peace be upon them. It is said that he was Sulaymān himself, peace be upon him, but this has a distance that is not hidden. By "the Book" is meant the genus that encompasses all the revealed books, or the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ). The indefiniteness of "ʿilm" (knowledge) is for magnification and to indicate that it is a knowledge not customarily known. And "min" is for origin (ibtidāʾiyya).

﴿Anā ātīka bihi qabla an yartadda ilayka ṭarfuka﴾ [I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you]. Al-ṭarf is the moving of the eyelids and their opening to look at something, and its ir-tidād (returning) is their closing. Because this is a natural matter not dependent on intention, ir-tidād was preferred over radd (return). And since there was no interval of any length between this promise and its fulfilment, as there was in the promise of the ʿifrīt, he dispensed with emphasis, and the mention of the bringing was elided in the narration, to signal that it is a matter certain and independent of being reported. The fāʾ al-fasīḥa (the eloquent fāʾ, which indicates an elided conditional clause) is used, not as entering upon a clause coordinated with a presumed clause indicating only its occurrence, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So We said, "Strike the sea with your staff," and it parted﴾ and its like, but rather it enters upon the conditional clause, where it is said: ﴿So when he saw it settled beside him﴾, that is, he saw the throne present before him, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So when they saw it, they considered it great...﴾. This is to show the complete manifestness of what was mentioned, its certain occurrence, and its independence from being reported, by making clear the manifestness of what follows from it, namely Sulaymān's, peace be upon him, seeing it, and he also dispenses with explicitly stating it. For the implied sense is: "So he brought it to him, and he saw it, and when he saw it..." etc. Thus what was elided was elided for the reasons mentioned, and to signal the complete swiftness of its bringing, as if nothing at all had occurred between the promise of it and his, peace and blessings be upon him, seeing it. In restricting his seeing it to its being settled beside him, peace and blessings be upon him, there is an emphasis on this meaning, because it gives the impression that no intermediate bringing occurred between them at all, as if it had always been present with him, along with what that implies of the lasting settledness of its being beside him, placed within the string of his kingdom.

﴿Qāla﴾ [He said], that is, Sulaymān, peace be upon him, receiving the blessing with gratitude, following the custom of the sons of his kind, from among the prophets of God, Exalted, and His pure servants, peace be upon them.

﴿Hādhā﴾ [This], that is, the presence of the throne before him in this brief period, or the capacity to bring it, whether by means or directly, as has been said, ﴿is of the bounty of my Lord﴾, that is, His favour upon me without any merit on my part.

﴿Liyabluwanī a-ashkuru﴾ [to test me: whether I am grateful], by seeing that it is pure bounty from Him, Exalted, without any power or strength from my side, and by fulfilling its due right. ﴿Am akfuru﴾ [or whether I am ungrateful], by finding for myself a place of entry in the matter, or by falling short in performing its obligations, as is the case with all the blessings that overflow upon the servants.

﴿Wa-man shakara fa-innamā yashkuru li-nafsihi﴾ [And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self], because by it his stored reward is bound to him, its increase is drawn, the burden of obligation is lifted from his responsibility, and he is freed from the stain of ingratitude.

﴿Wa-man kafara﴾ [And whoever is ungrateful], that is, does not give thanks, ﴿fa-inna Rabbī ghaniyyun﴾ [then indeed my Lord is Self-sufficient] regarding his gratitude, ﴿karīm﴾ [Generous], by deferring the punishment and bestowing favours even with the absence of gratitude as well.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 41:

﴿He said﴾, that is, Sulayman (peace be upon him). The narration is repeated although what is related is both before and after his words (peace be upon him), to draw attention to the difference between the earlier and the later part, since the first is an expression of thanks to God, the Exalted, and the second is a command to his servants: ﴿Disguise her throne for her﴾, that is, alter its form in some way.

﴿We will see﴾ is in the jussive mood, as a response to the imperative (jawab al-amr), and it has been read in the indicative as a resumption (al-istinaf). ﴿Whether she will be guided﴾ to knowing it, or to the appropriate answer for the occasion. It has been said: to belief in God, the Exalted, and His Messenger upon seeing it, because her throne had been brought from a great distance in a short time, while she had left it locked behind doors, with guards and chamberlains assigned to it. (p-288) However, the linking of the looking, which is tied to being guided, to the disguising is contrary to this, since that has no bearing on the disguising.

﴿Or will she be﴾, that is, relative to our knowledge, ﴿among those who are not guided﴾, that is, to what has been mentioned of knowing her throne, or to the correct answer. For although her being among them in reality is a continuing matter, her being among them in the sight of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and his people is a new matter that becomes apparent through testing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 42:

﴿So when she arrived﴾ This begins the narration of the test that Solomon, peace be upon him, intended.
