That is: when Bilqis arrived before Solomon, peace be upon him, and the throne was before him, ﴿it was said﴾, that is, by Solomon, peace be upon him, either directly or through an intermediary, ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾ He did not say, "Is this your throne?" lest it be a suggestion to her, so that the purpose of the command, which was by the indefinite form, would be lost. The purpose was to present the throne in a context of confusion and uncertainty, until her condition became clear. It has been mentioned that she had spoken in his presence, peace be upon him, about the weakness of intellect.

﴿She said, "It is as though it were it"﴾ Thus she showed the perfection of the soundness of her intellect, in that she did not say, "It is it," although she knew the reality of the situation. This hinted at the kind of difference in attributes that he had acquired through the indefinite form, while the essence remained the same, and out of regard for good manners in her address to him, peace be upon him.

﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims."﴾ This is part of her speech. It is as though she thought that he, peace be upon him, intended by this to test her intellect and to display a miracle for her. So she said: we were given knowledge of the perfect power of God, Exalted, and of the truth of your prophethood before this miracle that we have witnessed, through what we heard from the one who warns (al-Mundhir) of the signs that point to that. ﴿And we were Muslims﴾ from that time. In this there is an indication of the perfection of the sobriety of her judgment and the soundness of her thought, which is not hidden.

And His saying, ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah hindered her﴾, is an explanation from Him, exalted is He, of what had been preventing her from openly displaying the Islam she had claimed until now. That is, her former worship of the sun hindered her from doing so.

And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾, is a causal explanation (ta'lil) of the causal link between the aforementioned worship and the hindrance. That is, she was from a people firmly rooted in disbelief, and for this reason she was not able to display her Islam while she was among them, until she came under the dominion of Sulayman (peace be upon him). It is also read as "أنَّها" (annahā, "that she") with a fatha, either as a substitute (badal) for the subject of "صَدَّ" (saddā, "hindered"), or as a causal explanation with the lām elided, meaning "because she". As for what has been said, that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"And we were given knowledge"...﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿…from a disbelieving people﴾, is part of the speech of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and his council, as though when they heard her saying ﴿as though it were it﴾, they perceived her Islam and said, out of approval of her affair: she was right in her answer, and she knew the power of Allah, exalted is He, and the truth of prophethood through what she had heard from the warner of the previous signs and what she had witnessed of this wondrous sign concerning her throne, and she was granted Islam. So they joined to that their saying ﴿"And we were given knowledge"...﴾, etc., meaning: we were given knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and of His power, and of the truth of what came from Him, before her knowledge, and we have remained upon the religion of Islam, thanking Allah, exalted is He, for His favour upon them and their precedence over her in knowing Allah, exalted is He, and in Islam before her; and that the worship of the sun, and her upbringing among the disbelievers, prevented her from advancing to Islam. Yet what is involved in this of remoteness and forced interpretation is not hidden.

(p-289)﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace."﴾ *Al-sarh* means a palace, and it was also said to mean the courtyard of a house. It is narrated that Sulayman, peace be upon him, had commanded, before her arrival, that a palace be built on her route, made of white glass, with water flowing beneath it and fish and other sea creatures placed in it. He set his throne in its center, and he sat upon it, while the birds, the jinn and the humans gathered around him. He did this so that she would be further awed by his affair, would be certain of his prophethood, and would be firm in the religion. They claimed that the jinn disliked his marrying her, lest she reveal their secrets to him, since she was the daughter of a jinn. It was also said that they feared he would have a child by her who would combine the cleverness of the jinn and the humans, and they would then leave Sulayman's dominion for a kingdom that was harsher and more terrible. So they said, "There is something wrong with her intellect, and she has hairy shins, and her foot is like the hoof of a donkey." So he tested her intellect by disguising the throne, and he built the palace so that he could see her shins and her foot.

﴿When she saw it﴾ while he was present before her, as the command to enter indicates, and she came to know its details through information.

﴿She thought it was a pool and bared her shins﴾ and she gathered up her skirts so that they would not get wet. Then, behold, she had the most beautiful shins and feet of all people, except that they were hairy. It was said that she was the cause of the use of *al-nura* (depilatory lime). He commanded the devils, and they made it for her, and he married her. He also commanded the jinn, and they built for her *Silahin* and *Ghimdan*. He would visit her once a month and stay with her for three days. It was also said that he actually married her to *Dhu Tubba'*, the king of Hamdan, and empowered him over Yemen, and he commanded Zawba'a, the emir of the jinn of Yemen, to obey him, and he built for him the *masani'* (reservoirs). It was also read as "*sa'aqiha*," treating the singular as plural, as in *su'q* and *as'uq* (both plural forms of the word for shin).

﴿He said﴾, peace be upon him, when he saw the astonishment and fear that had overcome her: ﴿Indeed, it﴾ that is, what she had supposed to be water, ﴿is a palace paved smooth﴾ that is, made smooth, ﴿of glass.﴾ That is, of crystal.

﴿She said﴾ when she witnessed this miracle as well: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself﴾ by what I was upon until now, of worshiping the sun. It was also said that it meant by her suspicion of Sulayman, since she thought he intended to drown her in the pool, though this is far-fetched.

﴿And I have submitted with Sulayman﴾ following him and taking him as a model. As for what is in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, there is a shift to the majestic Name and a description of Him with the lordship over the worlds, to manifest her knowledge of His divinity, His exclusive entitlement to worship, and His lordship over all existing things, of which the sun she had been worshiping before that is a part.

﴿And We had certainly sent﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly given David and Solomon knowledge...﴾. It is brought in for the same purpose for which that was brought, namely the affirmation that he, upon him be peace, is being given the Qur'an from the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing, for this story too is part of the noble Qur'an which he, upon him be peace, received. The lam is the answer to an omitted oath, i.e., "By God, We had certainly sent to Thamud their brother Ṣāliḥ."

The ʾan in His statement, ﴿that worship God﴾, is either explanatory (mufassira) of the sense of saying contained in "sending", or it is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya) from which the preposition bāʾ has been dropped. It was also read with a ḍamma on the nūn, to match the bāʾ.

﴿Then behold, they became two factions disputing﴾: so they were suddenly split into factions and in dispute, whereby one faction believed and one faction disbelieved. The wāw (and) refers to the two factions taken together.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 46:

﴿He said﴾ — upon him be prayer and peace — to the disbelieving faction among them, after he had witnessed from them what he had witnessed of extreme obstinacy and stubbornness, to the point that they reached such brazenness that they said to him, upon him be prayer and peace, "O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful." ﴿O my people, why do you seek to hasten the evil before the good?﴾ That is: by the evil punishment, ﴿before the good﴾, that is: the repentance, so that you postpone it until the time of its descent. For they, because of their ignorance and their misguidance, used to say: "If his threat comes to pass, we will repent at that time; otherwise, we will remain as we were."

﴿Why do you not ask forgiveness of Allah﴾ — why do you not ask forgiveness of Him, exalted is He, before its descent — ﴿that you may be shown mercy?﴾ — by its acceptance, since there is no possibility of acceptance at the time of descent.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 47:

﴿They said: "We have taken omen from you"﴾. Its original form is "تَطَيَّرْنا" (tatayyarnā), and al-taṭayyur (ill omen-taking, the drawing of omens from birds) means al-tashā'um (taking an ill omen). It was expressed by this word because they, when they set out travelling, would pass by a bird and drive it away. If it passed on their right (sānihan), they took it as good omen, and if it passed on their left (bāriḥan), they took it as bad omen. When they attributed good and evil to the bird, the word was borrowed for that which was the cause of both, from the decree of God Most High and His apportionment, or from the action of the servant. That is: "We take an ill omen from you" ﴿and from those with you﴾ in your religion, since hardships followed one another upon us, and they had suffered drought. "And have we not been in disagreement and division since you invented your religion?"

﴿He said: "Your omen"﴾, that is, your cause, from which there befalls you what befalls you of evil, ﴿is with God﴾, and it is His decree, or your deeds recorded with Him. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾, that is, you are being tried by the alternation of ease and hardship, or you are being punished, or Satan tempts you by his whispering to you the ill omen. The turn to "rather" (iḍrāb) is a shift from explaining their omen, which is the origin of what befalls them, to mentioning that which calls them to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 48:

﴿And there were in the city﴾, namely al-Hijr, ﴿nine men (rahṭ)﴾, i.e., persons. It is on this basis that it came as a specifier (tamyiz) for "nine" (tis'ah), not on the basis of its wording. The difference between it (rahṭ) and nafar is that rahṭ is used from three or seven up to ten, whereas nafar is used from three up to nine. Their names, as transmitted from Wahb, were: al-Hudhayl ibn 'Abd Rabb, Ghunm ibn Ghanam, Ri'ab ibn Muharij, Misda' ibn Muharij, 'Umayr ibn Kurdubah, 'Asim ibn Makhramah, Subayt ibn Sadaqah, Sham'an ibn Safi, and Qudar ibn Salif. They are the ones who undertook the slaughter of the she-camel, and they were the most obstinate of the people of Salih, and they were from among the sons of their nobles.

﴿They spread corruption in the land﴾, not in the city alone, corruption that is pure, unmixed with any trace of reform, as His words, exalted be He, indicate: ﴿and they do not reform﴾, i.e., they do not do any act of reform, or they do not reform anything of [any] things.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 49:

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining some of the corruption they committed, meaning: some of them said to others, in the course of their consultation, concerning a matter of Salih (peace be upon him), and this was after he had warned them of the punishment (al-'adhb). And his saying: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days...﴾ and so on.

﴿Swear to one another by God﴾ may be either a command in the form of speech (amr maqul) governed by ﴿they said﴾, or a past-tense verb that stands in apposition to it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, with "qad" implied. His Exalted saying: ﴿that we will surely attack him and his family﴾ means: that we will surprise Salih and his family by night and surely kill them. It is also read with the ta' (lantubayyitanna), as an address from some of them to others, and it is read with the ya' of the third person and a ḍammah on the ta' (layubayyitunna), so that taqasamu is a past-tense verb.

﴿Then we will surely say to his heir﴾ means: to the heir of Salih. It is read with ta' and ya', as the previous one is.

﴿We did not witness the destruction of his people﴾ means: we were not present at their destruction, or at the time of their destruction, or at the place of their destruction, let alone that we would take charge of their annihilation. It is also read *mahlaka* with a fatḥah on the lam, in which case it is a verbal noun (maṣdar).

﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾ is part of the speech, or a circumstantial clause, meaning: we say what we say, and the circumstance is that we are truthful in that, because the one who witnesses something is, by custom, not the one who directly carries it out; or because we did not witness his destruction alone, but his destruction and theirs together, like your saying: "I did not see a man there, but two men."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 50:**

﴿And they plotted a plot﴾ by this agreement, ﴿and We plotted a plot﴾ — that is, We destroyed them with a destruction unlike any usual one — ﴿while they did not perceive﴾. Or, We requited their plot upon them from where they did not expect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 51:

﴿So look at how was the end result of their scheming﴾ This begins an explanation of what followed from the scheming they had undertaken, and how the clause "how" (kayfa) is dependent on the verb of looking (al-nazar). The clause occupies the accusative position by omission of the preposition (naz' al-khafid), meaning: "So reflect on how the end result of their scheming was." And His, exalted is He, saying ﴿that We destroyed them﴾ is either an appositive (badal) for ﴿the end result of their scheming﴾, with the phrase being the subject (fa'il) of "was," where "was" is a complete verb (tammah) and "how" is a circumstantial accusative (hal). That is: "So look at how it came about," meaning, in what manner Our destruction of them occurred. Or it is the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject (mubtada'), and the clause explains the vagueness (al-ibham) in ﴿the end result of their scheming﴾, meaning: it is Our destruction of them ﴿and their people﴾, those who were not with them in the act of plotting the night attack, ﴿all of them﴾, such that not one of them escaped. Or it is a causal clause (ta'lil) for what the command to look at the manner of the end result of their scheming indicates, of extreme horror and dreadfulness, with the preposition deleted, meaning: "because We destroyed them, etc."

It has been said that "was" is an incomplete verb (naqisah), its subject being ﴿the end result of their scheming﴾ and its predicate ﴿how was﴾. In that case the most suitable reading is that ﴿"that We destroyed them"..﴾ etc. is a causal explanation of what was mentioned.

It was also read as "Inna dammarnahum" etc. with a kasra, as a resumed sentence (isti'naf).

It is narrated that Salih, peace be upon him, had a place of worship in al-Hijr, in a ravine, where he would pray. They said: "Salih claims that he will finish with us within three days, so we will finish with him and his family before the three days." So they went out to the ravine and said: "When he comes to pray, we will kill him; then we will return to his family and kill them." So God, exalted is He, sent a rock from the mountain opposite them, and they hurried, and the rock closed over them at the mouth of the ravine. Their people did not know where they were, and they did not know what had been done to their people. God, exalted is He, punished each of them in his place, and saved Salih and those who were with him.

It has been said: they came at night with their swords drawn, and God, exalted is He, had sent the angels to fill Salih's house, and they struck them with stones; they saw the stones but did not see the one throwing them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 52:

﴿So those are their houses﴾, a sentence confirming what precedes it. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ruined﴾, i.e., empty, or fallen down and demolished. ﴿Because of what they did wrong﴾, i.e., because of their aforementioned wrongdoing; it is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "their houses," and the operative element in it is the meaning of the demonstrative ("those").  It has also been read as "khawiyatun" (in the nominative), on the basis that it is a predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf).

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in what has been mentioned of the wondrous destruction on account of their wrongdoing, ﴿is a sign﴾, a great lesson, ﴿for a people who know﴾. That is, [it is a sign for] whoever is of such a nature as to know anything of things, or [it is a sign] for a people characterized by knowledge.

And We delivered those who believed, [Salih] and those with him among the believers, ﴿and they used to be wary of (taqwa)﴾, that is, of disbelief and sins, with continuous wariness; therefore they were singled out for deliverance.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 54:**

﴿Lūṭan﴾ (And Lot) is in the accusative, governed by a concealed verb coordinated with "We sent" (arsalnā) at the beginning of the story of Ṣāliḥ, and it falls under the same oath together with him, meaning: "And We sent Lot." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when he said to his people﴾ is an adverbial clause (ẓarf) for the sending, on the basis that what is meant by it is an extended matter in which the sending took place, along with what passed between him and his people of words and circumstances. It has also been said that the accusative of Lot is by the concealed verb "remember" (udhkur), and "when" (idh) is a substitute (badal) for it. It has also been said that it is coordinated with "those who believed," meaning "and We saved Lot," but this is remote.

﴿Do you indeed commit the immorality﴾, that is, the deed that is extreme in ugliness and vileness. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿while you see﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah) from the subject of "you commit," serving to emphasize the denunciation and intensify the reproach, for committing an ugly act while knowing its ugliness is even more abominable and shameful. "You see" (tubṣirūn) is from the sight of the heart, meaning: "Do you do it while you know with certain knowledge that it is so?" It has also been said that some of you see it in others, since they used to openly practise it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 55:

﴿Must you really approach men lustfully, instead of women?﴾ This is a repetition for the sake of denunciation, a reiteration for the sake of reproach, and an explanation of the indecency they commit by way of explicit statement. The clause is embellished with the two particles of emphasis (ḥarfā al-ta'kīd) to signal that its content is something no one would believe to have occurred, owing to its utter remoteness from sound reason. The object is mentioned under the title of manhood (ar-rujūliyyah) in order to foster the abhorrence of the act and to establish the contrast between it and the lust which was given as the reason for the approach. ﴿Instead of women﴾ means: passing beyond the women, who are the loci of desire.

﴿Nay, you are a people who act in ignorance﴾ means: you act as ignorant people do in regard to its ugliness; or, you are ignorant of the consequence; or "ignorance" is used in the sense of frivolity and debauchery, i.e. "Nay, you are a people who are foolish and dissolute." The ta' in "tajhalūn" is here, although it is an attribute of "qawm" (people), because they are within the scope of address.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 56:

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lut from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ (They keep themselves aloof from our deeds, or from the filth, and they consider our deed to be filth.) And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was mockery. It has already passed in (Surat al-A'raf) that this answer was what proceeded from them at the last of the occasions of Lut's admonitions, through command and prohibition, not that no other speech proceeded from them besides it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 57:

﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; We had decreed that she would be among those who remained behind.﴾ That is: We decreed that she would be ﴿among those who remained behind﴾, i.e., those who remained in the punishment.

"And We rained upon them a rain" (a rain unlike any customary one), "so evil was the rain of those who were warned." The manner of the punishment that befell them has been explained more than once already.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 59:

﴿Say: "Praise be to God, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ This follows God Most High's recounting to His Messenger ﷺ the stories of the prophets mentioned, may blessings and peace be upon them, and their accounts, which declare the perfection of His power and the greatness of His majesty, and the signs that compel and the striking miracles He granted them, which indicate the exalted rank of these prophets and the soundness of their reports. Through their tongues He made clear the truth of Islam and of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and the falsehood of disbelief and shirk (associating partners with God), and that whoever follows them has been guided, and whoever turns away from them has fallen into the abysses of destruction. He expanded the chest of the Messenger ﷺ with the various kinds of divine knowledge contained within those stories, and illuminated his heart with the lights of the holy qualities that overflow from the world of holiness. Through this, He confirmed the substance of what His saying, Mighty and Majestic, expressed: ﴿And indeed you are receiving the Qur'an from One who is Wise and All-Knowing.﴾ He commanded him, peace and blessings be upon him, to praise Him for the blessings He bestowed upon him, beyond which no aspirant has any object of desire and no aspirer has any goal, and to greet with peace all the prophets, among whom are those whose stories were recounted to him. These stories are among the knowledge that became incumbent upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, in fulfilment of the right of their precedence and their striving in religion. It has also been said: this is a command to Lot, peace be upon him, to praise Him for destroying the disbelievers of his people, and to greet with peace the one whom He chose by preserving him from immoralities and saving him from destruction. But its remoteness is not hidden.

﴿Is God better, or what they associate with Him?﴾ That is: is God, whose great affairs have been mentioned, better, or what they make partners with Him, of idols? The purpose of this questioning is to rebuke the disbelievers on God's behalf, to belittle their feeble opinions, and to mock them. For it is evident that there is no trace of good whatsoever in what they have associated with Him, so that it could be weighed against One from whom there is no good except His good, and there is no god but Him. It has been read as "tushrikūna" (you associate), with the second-person form, by way of iltifat (shifting of address) and directing the speech to the disbelievers. This is more fitting to what follows in the noble context, which is built upon addressing them. Taking it as part of the speech commanded to be said is refuted by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We caused to grow…﴾ and so on, for this is clear that the rebuke comes directly from Him, Mighty and Majestic. Interpreting it as a report from him, peace and blessings be upon him, of what he was commanded to say in his own words, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves…"﴾, is an evident forced interpretation without any reason calling for it.

The "am" in His words ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth?﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'a). The "bal" implied in it, according to the first recitation, serves to shift (al-darb wa'l-intiqal, lit. "striking and transitioning") from rebuke (al-tabkit) to the explicit statement, addressed directly, in a manner more evident than before, for greater emphasis and intensity. As for the second recitation, it serves to repeat the rebuke and reiterate the charge, like its similar occurrences that follow. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for establishing their admission (taqrir), meaning: bringing them to acknowledge the truth out of necessity, for no one who has even minimal discernment can restrain himself or refrain from acknowledging the superiority of the One who created all creatures and bestowed upon each of them what suits it of its benefits, from the lowliest and most insignificant of those creatures, and indeed (bal) that there is no good seen in it in any respect whatsoever, definitively. "Man" is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, together with the equivalent "am" (mu'adilah) to the hamza, relying on what preceded in the first interrogation. Except that "tushrikun" here is with the second-person ta' in both recitations, and likewise in the four subsequent places. The meaning: "Rather, who originated the creation of the two regions of the physical world and the sources of the benefits that lie between them?"

﴿And sent down for you﴾ is a shift (iltifat) to address the disbelievers in the first recitation, to intensify the rebuke and the charge, meaning: He sent down for your sake and your sustenance ﴿from the sky water﴾, meaning a kind of it, namely rain, ﴿then We caused to grow thereby gardens﴾, meaning enclosed orchards surrounded by walls, ﴿full of delight﴾, meaning possessing beauty and splendor by which onlookers rejoice. ﴿It was not for you﴾, meaning it was not right nor possible for you ﴿to cause their trees to grow﴾, let alone their fruit and the rest of their wondrous attributes. [Is He] better, or what you associate [with Him]? It is also recited "amana" with a lightened hamza, as a substitution (badal) for "Allah", and the fronting of the two complements of "sent down" before its object is for the reason repeatedly mentioned, namely to create suspense until the postponed element arrives. The shift to the first person in His words ﴿"then We caused to grow"﴾ serves to emphasize that the act is exclusively attributed to His Essence, and to signal that causing those gardens of differing kinds, attributes, colors, tastes, scents and shapes, along with their excellent beauty and wondrous splendor, to grow from one water is something that scarcely anyone can accomplish except Him alone, as indicated by restricting them with His words ﴿"It was not for you"﴾ etc. Whether this is an attribute of them or a circumstantial clause (hal). The singular of their first attribute, namely "full of delight", is because the meaning is "a group of gardens full of delight", following the pattern of their saying "the women went", and likewise the situation regarding the pronoun in "their trees".

﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, meaning: is there another god alongside Allah, who has had mentioned some of His acts which almost no one other than Him can accomplish, to the point that one might imagine making him a partner to Him in worship? This is a rebuke to them by negating divinity from what they associate with Him, within the general negation, in the demonstrative manner, after rebuking them by negating goodness from him through the enumeration mentioned. For just as anyone who has some discernment cannot deny that goodness is entirely absent from him, he can hardly deny that divinity is absent from him altogether, especially after considering that its properties are absent from all besides Him, the Exalted. The situation is the same in the four subsequent positions. It has been said: the intended meaning is the negation that there is with Him, Exalted is He, another god in what has been mentioned of creation and what is joined to it, but not in the sense that the rebuke is by that negation alone, for how could it be, since they do not deny it, as His words indicate: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾. Rather, by their associating others with Him, Exalted is He, in worship, they acknowledge that He has no partner in what has been mentioned of the necessary attributes of divinity. It is as if it were said: "Is there another god with Allah in the special properties of divinity, such that he is made a partner to Him, Exalted is He, in worship?" It has also been said: the meaning is: is his other than Him associated with Him and made a partner in worship, despite His sole creative and originating power? Thus the interrogation is for reproach and rebuke along with establishing the denied matter, not merely negation, as in the two previous interpretations. The first is the most evident and agrees with His words ﴿And there is not with Him any god...﴾, and it is most fitting to the context, since it conveys the negation of the existence of another god alongside Him, Exalted is He, altogether, not merely the negation of His being with Him in creation and its branches. It is also recited "a'ilahun" with an intermediate madda between the two hamzas, and with the second hamza pronounced between-between (bayna bayn). It is also recited "a'ilahan", with an implied verb suited to the context, such as: "Do you call upon?" or "Do you associate?"

﴿Rather, they are a people who deviate﴾. This is a turning away (idrab) and a transition from rebuking them through direct address to explaining the evil of their condition and reporting it to others. Meaning: rather, they are a people whose habit is to deviate entirely from the path of truth and to swerve from uprightness in every matter; therefore they do what they do, deviating from the clear truth, which is monotheism, and clinging to manifest falsehood, which is associating partners. It has been said: "they make others equal to Him, Exalted is He", but this is far-fetched and devoid of benefit.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 61:

﴿Is He not [best] who made the earth a stable resting place﴾. It has been said: this is a substitution (badal) for "Or who created the heavens..." and so on, and likewise the three clauses that follow it; the ruling for all of them is one. The more evident view is that each of them is a transition (idrab wa intiqal) from rebuking with what preceded it to rebuking with another aspect that is more binding as an obligation from one of the directions, i.e., He made it such that humans and animals can settle upon it, by [the] raising of some of it above the water, and by its spreading out (dahw) and leveling (taswiyah), as their benefits require.

﴿And He made within it rivers﴾, i.e., in its midst (awsat), flowing, [from] which they benefit (p-295) ﴿and He made for it firm mountains﴾, i.e., immovable mountains that prevent it from shaking with its inhabitants, in which minerals form, from whose lowlands springs gush forth, and to which are attached countless benefits.

﴿And He made between the two seas﴾, i.e., the sweet and the salt, or the two gulfs of Persia and Rome, ﴿a barrier﴾, a isthmus (barzakh) preventing intermixing. This has been discussed in Surat al-Furqan. The "making" (ja'l) in the last three positions is creative (ibda'i), and the placing of its object after the adverbial phrase is for the sake of creating suspense (tashwiq), as has been noted many times.

﴿Is there a god along with Allah?﴾ in existence, or "or" in originating these wonders, as has been explained. ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾, i.e., anything of things, and therefore they do not understand the falsehood of the polytheism they hold, despite its complete clarity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 62:

﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him,﴾ that is, the one whom a severe hardship has brought to need and has compelled to seek refuge and to humble supplication before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is the past participle (ism maf'ul) of al-idtirar (being compelled), which is an iftti'al form derived from al-darurah (necessity). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "It is the one who is afflicted (al-majhud)." And it is reported from al-Suddi, may Allah have mercy on him: "The one who has no power and no strength." It has also been said: "The sinner when he seeks forgiveness." The lam here is for the genus (li-l-jins), not for comprehensiveness (li-l-istighraq), so that it would not necessitate the response to every distressed person.

﴿and removes the evil﴾, which is what befalls a person of the things that distress him, ﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾, that is, successors in it, by granting you its inhabitation and its disposal after the peoples who came before you. It has also been said that what is meant by succession (khilafah) is sovereignty and dominion.

﴿Is there a god along with Allah?﴾ He who bestows upon all mankind these great blessings. ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, that is, a little remembrance, or a short time in which you remember. The "ma" is superfluous, serving to emphasize the meaning of paucity, which is intended to mean nonexistence, or something that takes its place in insignificance and uselessness. In concluding the discourse with the negation of remembrance from them, there is an indication that its content is fixed in the mind of every intelligent and dull person alike, and that it is so evident that it requires nothing beyond turning attention to it and recalling it. It has been read as "tatadhakkarun" according to the original form, and as "tadhdhakkarun" and "yudhakkirun" (with ta' and ya') with idgham (assimilation).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 63:

﴿Or who guides you through the darknesses of the land and the sea?﴾ That is, through the darknesses of the nights in them, on the basis that the idafa (genitive construction) here is one of association (mulabasa); or [it means] through the confusing paths. It is said: "a tariqa zalma'" and "a tariqa 'amya'" (a dark or blind road) for the one that has no landmark (manar) in it.

﴿And who sends the winds as heralds of good news before His mercy?﴾ This is the rain. Even if it is established that the most common cause in the formation of wind is the recurrence of the vapours rising from the cold layer, their heat broken and their agitation of the air, there is no doubt that the efficient and receptive causes of all of that are among the creation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the one who produces a cause is definitely the one who produces what is caused.

﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ This is a negation that there should be another god with Him. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾ is an affirmation and confirmation of this, and the placing of the noble Name in the position of the pronoun serves to indicate the reason for the ruling. That is: exalted and far above, by His essence, which is singled out for divinity, entailing all attributes of perfection and qualities of beauty and majesty, which require that all creatures be subjugated under His power, [He is exalted] above what they associate with Him; that is, above the existence of what they associate with Him, Exalted is He, not absolutely (for its existence is something that cannot be denied), but rather above its existence under the title of being a god and a partner to Him, Exalted is He, or above their associating [it with Him].

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 64:

﴿Is He not (better) who originates creation and then repeats it?⦆ That is: Rather, is it not He who originates creation and then repeats it after death, by resurrection? ﴿And who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ That is: through heavenly and earthly causes which He has arranged in a wondrous order required by the wisdom upon which the affair of creation was founded. ﴿Is there a god﴾ other (than Allah) existing ﴿with Allah?﴾ so that he might be made a partner to Him in worship. His exalted words: ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾ are a command to him, upon him be prayers and peace, to rebuke them after a rebuke, that is: bring a rational or traditional proof which indicates that there is with Him, exalted is He, a god, not that another besides Him, exalted is He, has power over anything of the acts mentioned of Him, exalted is He, as has been said. For they do not explicitly call upon him, nor do they acknowledge that his existence is among the necessary attributes of divinity, although in reality it is among them; so demanding proof for it, rather than for their explicit claim, is without basis. And the attribution of the proof to their pronoun carries a mockery of them, because of what it implies, namely that they have a proof, and how could they have that?

﴿If you are truthful﴾, that is: in that claim.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 65:

﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah.﴾ Having established His exclusive divinity (uluhiyyah) by demonstrating that He alone possesses complete and perfect power and all-encompassing, universal mercy, He follows this with what is among its necessary consequences, namely His exclusive knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb). This completes what came before and prepares the ground for what follows concerning the matter of resurrection (al-ba'th). The exception (al-istithna') is disjunctive (munqati'), and the noun following the exception is in the nominative (raf') according to the Tamimi dialect (al-lughah al-tamimiyyah), to indicate the impossibility of knowing the unseen on the part of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, by making it contingent upon His being, glorified and exalted is He, one of them. It is as if it were said: If Allah, exalted is He, is among those in them, then among them there is one who knows the unseen. Or it is connected (muttasil), on the basis that what is meant by "those in the heavens and the earth" is whoever has knowledge encompassing them and who perceives them with the perception of one present within them; for this is a general metaphorical meaning applicable to Him, exalted is He, and to the possessors of knowledge among His creation. The word "man" (man) is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a descriptive (mawsufah).

﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ That is: when they will be raised from the graves, even though this is something of which they cannot be free and among the most important of matters to them. The word "ayyan" (ayyan) is composed of "ay" (ay) and "an" (an). It has also been read with a kasrah on the hamzah, and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, although the lack of awareness of what has been mentioned is general, lest it entail a disjunction between it and the pronouns that follow which are definitively specific to them. It has also been said: the whole refers to "man," and the attribution of the distinctive traits of the disbelievers to all of them is of the same kind as their saying: "The sons of so-and-so did such-and-such," when the doer is only some of them.

﴿Nay, their knowledge has overtaken [them] concerning the Hereafter.﴾ When He negated from them the knowledge of the Unseen, and affirmed this by negating their awareness of the time of what is inevitably their destination, the negation was emphasized and established further by turning away from it and making clear that they are in a greater ignorance than their ignorance of the time of their resurrection, since they do not know the states of the Hereafter at all, even though the means of knowing it are abundant. As for the meaning of ﴿ادّارَكَ عِلْمُهم في الآخِرَةِ﴾ ("their knowledge has overtaken [them] concerning the Hereafter"): their knowledge has been followed up and continued regarding the matter of the Hereafter, of which the resurrection mentioned is one of its states, until it was cut off and nothing of their knowledge remained of what will occur in it, decisively. However, this is not in the sense that they had true knowledge of it which then gradually ceased; rather it is in the manner of metaphor (majaz), by treating the causes and beginnings of knowledge, namely the rational and transmitted proofs, as if they were knowledge itself, and treating their gradual disappearance from the level of their consideration, each time they noticed them, as their successive progression toward cessation. Then He turned away and moved from explaining their lack of knowledge of it to explaining what is worse than that, namely their bewilderment in it, where it is said: ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about it﴾, meaning: in a dubious doubt about the Hereafter itself and its reality, like one who is bewildered in a matter for which he finds no proof, let alone the matters that will occur in it. Then He turned away from that to explain that what they are in is more severe and more atrocious than doubt, where it is said: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾, such that they can scarcely perceive its proofs, because their insight is completely corrupted.

It has been read: "بَلْ أدَّرِكَ عِلْمُهُمْ" (bal Addaraka ʿilmuhum), with the meaning: it ended and perished. Al-Hasan al-Basri (Hasan al-Basri) explained it as: their knowledge has vanished.

It has also been said: both forms are on their apparent meaning, i.e., their knowledge has been completed and firmly established, or the means of their knowledge that the Resurrection is certainly coming, by the decisive signs and the clear proofs, were complete, and they had attained knowledge to an extraordinary degree, while they remained ignorant in that. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about it﴾ is a turning away and a shift from describing them with absolute ignorance to describing them with doubt. His saying: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾ is a turning away from describing them with doubt to describing them with what is worse than it and more atrocious than blindness.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of describing them with the establishment and completion of knowledge is mockery of them, so it is a description of them with ignorance by way of emphasis, and the two turnings are as mentioned.

The root of ادّارَكَ is تَدارَكَ (tadaraka), and Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Kaʿb) read with it, so the tāʾ was changed into dāl and it was made sukūn, so the initial could not be pronounced, and the hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza) was brought in, becoming ادّارَكَ. It has been read: "بَلِ ادَّرَكَ" (bali Addaraka), whose original form is افْتَعَلَ (iftaʿala). And "بَلْ أأدَّرِكُ" with two hamzas; "بَلْ آأدْرَكَ" with an alif between them; "بَلْ أدْرَكَ" with lightening and transposition (naql); "بَلِ ادَّرَكَ" with a fatḥa on the lām and shaddah on the dāl, whose original is "بَلْ أدَّرَكَ" in the interrogative sense; "بَلى ادَّرَكَ", "بَلى أأدْرَكَ", "أمْ تَدارَكَ", and "أمِ ادَّرَكَ". These are twelve readings. Whatever contains an explicit interrogative, or one implied from it, is a denial and negation. Whatever contains "بَلى" is an affirmation of their awareness, and an explanation of it by perception in the manner of mockery, which is the most eloquent form of negation and denial. What follows it is a turning away from the explanation, for emphasis in negation and to indicate that their awareness of it is that they are in doubt about it, and then indeed they are blind to it; or it is a rejection and denial of their awareness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 67:

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾ is an explanation of their ignorance of the Hereafter and their bewilderment concerning it, by relating their denial of the Resurrection. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is placed in the position of their pronoun in order to censure them by what lies within its relative clause (silah), and to indicate the cause of their false judgment in their saying: ﴿When we have become dust, and our fathers too, shall we indeed be brought forth?﴾ That is: shall we be brought out from the graves when we have become dust, as the word "mukhrijun" (brought forth) indicates. It is not admissible for the verb "idha" (when) to be governed by this same verb (i.e., by "mukhrijun"), because several obstacles converge, any one of which alone would suffice to prevent it. The restriction of the bringing forth to the time of their being dust is not meant to limit the denial to bringing forth at that time only, for they deny the revival after death absolutely, even if the body remains in its state; rather, it is meant to strengthen the denial by directing it to the bringing forth in a state that is contrary to it. As for His saying, exalted is He: "and our fathers" (wa-aba'una), it is a conjunction upon the subject of "kunna" (we were), and the separation by the predicate has taken the place of separation by emphasis. The repetition of the interrogative particle in "a-innna" (shall we indeed) is for intensification and emphasis in the denial. The adornment of the sentence with "inna" (indeed) and the lam is for emphasizing the denial, not for denying the emphasis, as the apparent wording may suggest; for the placing of the interrogative hamza at the front is because it requires initial position, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ and its like, according to the view of the majority, since their meaning is that the denial follows (ta'qib al-inkar), not the denial of the following, as is well known.

(p-298) It is also read "idha kunna" with a single broken hamza, and it is read "inna lamukhrajun" as a declarative statement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 68:

﴿Indeed we and our fathers have been promised this﴾, i.e., the bringing forth (from the graves). ﴿Before this, we and our fathers﴾, i.e., before its promise by him, upon him be prayer and peace. The placing of "the promised" (al-mawʿud) before "we" is because it is the intended object of mention; and where it is delayed (as in the verse), what is intended is the one sent (al-mabʿuth). The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to affirm the denial, and its opening with the oath (al-qasam) is for further emphasis.

And His Exalted saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ is an affirmation following an affirmation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 69:

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and see how was the end of the criminals.﴾ This is because of their denial of the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, regarding what they called them to: belief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, alone, and in the Last Day, which you deny. For in witnessing their end there is sufficiency for those endowed with insight (ulu al-absar). And in describing the deniers as "criminals" there is a kindness to the believers, leading them to abandon crimes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 70:

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ due to their persistence in disbelief and denial. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾ in constriction of the breast ﴿because of what they plot﴾ from their scheming. Indeed, Allah the Exalted protects you from the people. It is also recited with a kasra on the dad (ḍīq), and this is likewise a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is permissible that the fatha-vowelled form be a lightened form of ḍīq, and it has indeed been recited thus, meaning: do not be in a tight matter.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 71:**

﴿And they say: "When is this promise,﴾ that is, the hastened punishment that was promised, ﴿if you are truthful?"﴾ in your report of its coming. The plural is used in consideration of the believers' sharing in the report of that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 72:

﴿Say: "It may be that some of what you are hastening for has drawn close to you (radifa lakum)."﴾ That is, it followed you and overtook you. The lam (lam) is extra, for emphasis, like the ba' (ba') in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. Or the verb is made to include the meaning of a verb that takes the lam as its object-marker. It is also read as radafa (with the dal vowelled with fatha), and this is a dialect (lughah) of the same verb.

﴿Some of that which you are hastening for﴾, and it is the punishment of the Day of Badr. The words 'asa (perhaps), la'alla (perhaps) and sawfa (surely/soon) in the promises of kings are equivalent to a firm affirmation, and they use them only to show dignity and to convey that a hint from people of their station is like a plain statement to others. The promise and threat of God, exalted is He, follow this same course. Choosing the wording of the noble Qur'an over saying "perhaps He will make it follow you" etc. is because it is more indicative of the certainty of the promise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 73:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind﴾. That is, He is truly bountiful and gracious toward all of mankind. Among the forms of His favor is His deferring the punishment of these people for the sins they commit, among which is their hastening of the punishment (istu'jal al-'adhab).

﴿But most of them do not give thanks﴾. They do not recognize the true worth of this blessing, so they do not thank Him for it; rather, out of their ignorance, they hasten its occurrence, as is the way of these people.

(p-299) ﴿And indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal﴾, i.e., what they hide. It is also read with a fatḥah on the tā', from kanantu al-shay', meaning I concealed the thing, when I covered it.

﴿And what they disclose﴾ of deeds and sayings, among which is what has been related of them concerning their seeking to hasten the punishment. In this is an indication that they have ugly qualities other than what they manifest, and that He, exalted is He, will requite them for all of it. As for the placing of the secret before the open, its wisdom has already been explained in (Surat al-Baqarah) at His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they disclose?﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 75:

﴿And there is not any hidden thing in the heaven and the earth﴾ i.e., there is no concealed thing within them. These two (heaven and earth) are among the attributes that prevail (al-sifat al-ghalibah), and the ta' (in ghaybah) is for emphasis (li-l-mubalaghah), as in riwayah (narration), or they are nouns for that which is absent and hidden. The ta' is for transferring the word to the category of nouns (li-l-naql ila al-ismiyyah).

﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾ i.e., clear (bayyin) or making clear (mubayyin) what is in it for whoever peruses it, and it is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). It has also been said that it is the just decree (al-qada' al-'adl), by way of metaphor (bi-tariq al-isti'arah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 76:

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.﴾ From among its scope is that they differed concerning the matter of the Messiah (al-Masih), split into factions (ahzab) regarding him, and mounted the back of arrogance (mat al-'utuw) and excess (al-ghuluww), going to extremes (al-ifrat) and deficiency (al-tafrit), in both likening (al-tashbih) and transcendence (al-tanzih). Among them arose mutual disputation (al-ta'akkud) over matters, until the contention reached the point where some of them cursed others. Yet the Noble Qur'an has descended to clarify the true reality of the matter, had they been within the sphere of fairness (inṣaf).

And indeed it is guidance and mercy for the believers (﴿وَإنَّهُ لَهُدًى ورَحْمَةٌ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾), without restriction, so that those among the Children of Israel who believed enter into them in the first and foremost sense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 78:

﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them﴾, i.e., between the Children of Israel, ﴿by His judgment﴾, by what He judges, and it is the truth; or by His wisdom (hikmah). This is supported by the fact that it was recited as "bi-hukmihi" (by His judgment).

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, so His judgment and decree are not reversed, ﴿the Knowing﴾ of all things, among which is what is decreed.

The fa' in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So put your trust in Allah﴾, is for the consequence of the command upon what has been mentioned of His affairs, glory be to Him and majesty be His. For these affairs make trust in Him obligatory and call to the command to do so. That is: "So put your trust in Allah, the One whose affair is such, for that makes it obligatory upon every person to put their trust in Him and to entrust all their affairs to Him."

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed you are upon the clear truth﴾, are an explicit reason (ta'lil) for trusting in Him, exalted is He, by the fact that He, peace and blessings be upon him, is upon the manifest truth, or the truth that separates him from falsehood, or that separates the one who is right from the one who is wrong. For his being upon the truth in this way is among the things that make one certain of His, exalted is He, protecting him, granting him victory and strengthening him without doubt.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 80:

(p-300) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾, etc. This is another justification for reliance upon God (tawakkul), which is an expression for devoting oneself wholly to God Most High (tabattul ila Allah), entrusting one's affair to Him, and turning away from clinging to anything other than Him. It was first justified by what it necessitates on God's part, namely His decree with truth, His might, and His knowledge, exalted is He. Second, it was justified by what it necessitates on the part of the Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace, in one of two respects, namely his being upon the truth, and on the part of God in the other respect, namely God's help and support for the one who is upon the truth. Third, it was justified by what it necessitates, though not directly but through its necessitating the turning away from clinging to anything other than God Most High. For their being like the dead, the deaf, and the blind necessitates cutting off all hope of their support and assistance entirely, and it calls for restricting reliance to God Most High, which is what is meant by trusting in God Most High. They were likened to the dead only because they are unaffected by what is recited to them of the striking warnings. The omission of the object of "make hear" indicates that they hear none of the things that are heard. Perhaps the intended meaning is to liken their hearts to the dead in the aforementioned lack of awareness, for the heart is one of the faculties of perception, and its nullity is indicated entirely, after which the nullity of the two faculties of the ear and the eye is made clear, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand, and they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear﴾. Otherwise, after likening themselves to the dead, there would be no further distinction in likening them to the deaf and the blind.

﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾, i.e., the summons to some matter. The restriction of the negation by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when they turn away retreating﴾ serves to complete the likeness and to emphasize the negation, for they, along with their deafness to the call to the truth, turn away from the caller and retreat on their heels. There is no doubt that the deaf person does not hear a call even when the caller is directly facing his ear and close to him, so how much more when the caller is behind him and far from him. It was also read: "and the deaf do not hear the call."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 81:

﴿Nor can you guide the blind away from their error﴾, with a guidance that conveys them to the desired goal, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾. For guidance is contingent upon sight. The particle "ʿan" (عَنْ) is connected to "guidance" in view of its implying the meaning of diverting (al-ṣarf). It was also said that it is connected to "blindness" (al-ʿamá), as one says ʿamá ʿan kadhā (he was blind to such-and-such), but this is far-fetched. The use of the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) is for emphasis in negating guidance.

It was also recited (qaraʾa, a recognized variant reading): "wa-mā anta tahdī al-ʿumyā" (وَما أنْتَ تَهْدِي العُمْيَ), meaning "Nor are you guiding the blind."

﴿If you make hear﴾, i.e., you do not make hear a hearing that benefits the listener, ﴿except those who believe in Our signs﴾, i.e., it is in their nature to believe in them. The mention of making hear, in both negation and affirmation, rather than guidance, despite their closeness, as if it were said: "You guide only those who believe in Our signs..." etc., is because the means of guidance is making the revealed signs heard.

﴿Then they are submitting﴾ is a reason for their believing in them, as if it were said: "For they are compliant with the truth." It was also said: they are sincere to God, from His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to God﴾.

[p-301] ﴿And when the word has come to pass against them﴾ explains what was alluded to by His saying, ﴿some of what you were hastening﴾, namely the rest of what they were hastening for of the Hour and its signs. By "the word" is meant what the noble verses had spoken of the coming of the Hour and of the various kinds of terrors that they used to hasten for. The expression "its coming to pass" (wuqu'uhu) refers to its establishment and occurrence. He expressed it thus to signal the severity of its impact and effect. Its attribution to "the word" is because the intent is to explain its occurrence insofar as it is the fulfilment of the speech that announced its coming. "Coming to pass" (al-wuquʿ) here means its nearness and approach, as in His saying, ﴿The command of God has come﴾ (16:1), meaning: when the occurrence of what the mentioned word signifies (al-madlul), which they hardly hear, and its fulfilment, draws near.

﴿We shall bring forth for them a beast from the earth﴾. It is al-Jassasa (the Spy-beast). The expression of it by a generic noun, and the emphasis on its indefiniteness by the magnifying tanwin (al-tanwin al-tafkhimi), indicates, as is not hidden, the strangeness of its condition and that its attributes are beyond the bounds of description. It has come in a hadith: "Its length is sixty cubits; the seeker cannot reach it, and the fleer cannot escape it." It is also related that it has four legs, and that it has down and feathers, and two wings. From Ibn Juraij concerning its description: a bull's head, a pig's eye, an elephant's ear, a stag's horn, an ostrich's neck, a lion's chest, a leopard's colour, a cat's flank, a ram's tail, a camel's hoof, and the distance between its two joints is twelve cubits by the cubit of Adam, upon him be peace. Wahb said: its face is the face of a man, and the rest of its creation is that of a bird. It is related from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "It is not a beast that has a tail, but it has a beard," as if alluding that it is a man. The well-known view, however, is that it is a beast. It is related that it will only come out with its head, and its head reaches the clouds of the sky or reaches the clouds. From Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him: in it is every colour, and the distance between its two horns is a farsakh for a rider. From al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him: its emergence will not be complete except after three days. From ʿAli, may God be pleased with him: it emerges over three days while people look on, and it does not emerge each day except a third of it.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked: "From where will the beast emerge?" He said: "From the most sacred of mosques before God, the Most High," meaning the Sacred Mosque. It is related that it emerges three emergences: it emerges at the farthest part of Yemen, then hides, then emerges in the desert, then hides for a long time. Then, while people are in the most sacred and honoured of mosques before God, the Most High, nothing terrifies them except its emergence from between the Corner, opposite the house of the Banu Makhzum, on the right of one leaving the mosque. Some people flee, and some stand as spectators. It was also said: it emerges from al-Safa. It is related that while ʿIsa, upon him be peace, was circling the House with the Muslims, the earth quakes beneath them like the shaking of a lamp, and al-Safa splits on the side near the place of running (al-Masʿa), and the beast emerges from al-Safa, and with it is the staff of Musa and the ring of Sulayman, upon them both be peace. It strikes the believer in his place of worship with the staff, and a white spot appears, which spreads until his face shines with it, and "Believer" is written between his eyes. It marks the disbeliever on the nose with the ring, and the spot spreads until his face turns black, and "Disbeliever" is written between his eyes. Then it says to them: "You, so-and-so, are of the people of Paradise, and you, so-and-so, are of the people of the Fire." It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he struck al-Safa with his staff while in a state of ihram, and said: "Indeed the beast hears the striking of this staff of mine."

Abu Hurayra related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Evil is the ravine, the ravine of Ajyad," twice or thrice. It was said: "Why is that, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The beast emerges from it, and it cries out three cries which whoever is between the two regions (of east and west) hears, and it speaks in Arabic with an eloquent tongue." This is His saying, ﴿it will speak to them that the people were not certain of Our signs﴾ (27:82), meaning: it will tell them that they were not certain of the signs of God, the Most High, which announce the coming of the Hour and its portents, or of all His signs, of which those signs are a part. It was also said: of His signs, of which its emergence before the Hour is a part. The first is the truth, as you will come to know fully. The recitation ("Inna al-nasa") and the attribution of the signs to the nun of majesty are because it is a report from Him, the Most High, of the meaning of its speech, not of its exact wording. It was also said: because it is a report from it of the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic. It was also said: because of its being specific to Him, the Most High, and its being cherished by Him, as some close courtiers of a king say: "Our horses and our lands," while the horses and lands truly belong to their master. It was also said: there is an omitted genitive construction, meaning: "with the signs of our Lord." Describing them as not being certain of them, while in fact they were denying them, signals that it was incumbent upon them to be certain of them and to affirm their truth, yet they were characterized by the opposite.

It has been recited as "Inna al-nasa" with the kasra, by implying a verb of saying (idmar al-qawl) or by treating the speech as if it were such; and the discussion of the attribution is as previously mentioned. It was also said: it is a new sentence (istiʾnaf) directed from Him, the Most High, to explain the emergence of the beast or its speaking. This is refuted by the combination of the past and the present tense forms, for it is explicit that it is a report of their former lack of certainty in the world. By "the people" is meant either the disbelievers in general, or the polytheists of Mecca. It is related from Wahb that it informs everyone who sees it that the people of Mecca were not certain of Muhammad and the Qur'an. It has been recited as "tukallimuhum" (wounds them) from al-kalm, which means wounding, and what is meant by it is the marking reported with the staff and the ring. It has been permitted that the well-known recitation may also be from this root, in the sense of intensification, but its remoteness is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 83:

﴿And on the Day when We gather from every nation a company﴾ is a general statement of the condition of the deniers at the establishment of the Hour, after the explanation of some of its preliminaries. "The Day" (yawma) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. What is meant by this gathering is the gathering for punishment, after the general gathering that encompasses all of creation. The directing of the command to remember the time, although the intent is to remind of the events that occur in it, has had its purpose explained many times. The meaning is: "And remember for them the time of Our gathering," that is, Our assembling, from every nation of the nations of the prophets, peace be upon them, or from the people of every generation of generations, a large group. Here "min" (from) is partitive, because every nation is divided into those who affirm and those who deny.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿of those who deny Our signs﴾ is an explanation of the company, that is, a company of those who deny them. ﴿Then they will be driven on⦄ meaning their first is held back until the last of them, so that they catch up with one another and gather at the place of rebuke and questioning. In this there is, of course, an indication of the abundance of their number and the spread of their extremities. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and Shayba ibn Rabi'a are driven ahead of the people of Makkah, and thus will the leaders of all the other nations be gathered before them into the Fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 84:

﴿Until, when they have come﴾ to the place of questioning, answer, debate and reckoning, ﴿He will say﴾; that is, God, Mighty and Majestic, rebuking them for their denial, and the shift [in speech] to the third person serves to cultivate awe: ﴿"Did you deny My signs"﴾ which speak of the meeting of this your Day? And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"while you did not encompass them in knowledge"﴾ is a circumstantial clause serving to increase the enormity of the denial and the extremity of its ugliness, and it reinforces the disavowal and the rebuke. That is: did you deny them at first glance, without looking into them with a look that leads to knowledge of their reality, and that they are indeed deserving of belief, necessarily? This is a clear indication that what is meant by "signs" in the two places mentioned earlier is the Qur'anic verses, because they are what contain the proofs of validity and the evidences of truthfulness, which they did not encompass in knowledge, although they were obliged to reflect and ponder upon them, not the Hour itself and what is in it. It has been said: it is coordinated with "you denied" [i.e., the meaning is]: you combined denial with failure to reflect upon them.

﴿"Or what was it that you were doing?"﴾ That is: or what was it that you were doing with them, or what was it that you were doing other than that, meaning: they had no action other than that, as if they had been created only for disbelief and sins, while in fact they were created only for faith and obedience; they are addressed with this as a rebuke.

Then they will be flung headlong into the Fire. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the word will be fulfilled against them﴾, meaning: the punishment that is the meaning of the spoken word has descended upon them and come down to them. ﴿Because of what they wronged﴾, that is, because of their wrongdoing, which is their denial of the signs of Allah. ﴿So they will not speak﴾, due to their being completely cut off from any answer, and their being afflicted with a preoccupying distraction of painful punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 86:

(p-303) ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest in it﴾. The seeing (al-ru'yah) here is of the heart (qalbiyyah), not of the eye (basariyyah), because the very nature of night and day, although they are among the perceptible things, yet making them as has been mentioned belongs to the category of intelligibles. That is: Have they not known that We made the night, with the darkness that is in it, so that they might rest in it through sleep and repose? ﴿And the day as something to see by﴾, that is, so that they might see by the light that is in it the paths of moving about in matters of livelihood. Hyperbole is employed here, for seeing, which is the state of people, is made a state of the day and one of its attributes, with which it was created, such that it never separates from it. He did not follow this same course with the night, because the effect of the darkness of the night on rest is not comparable to the effect of the light of day on sight.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, in Our making them as they have been described, and the meaning of distance in the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) serves to indicate the remoteness of their rank in excellence, ﴿are signs﴾, that is, great and numerous signs, ﴿for a people who believe﴾, indicating with clear proof the soundness of the Resurrection and the truth of the verses that declare it. How could it not be so, for whoever reflects on the succession of night and day and their alternation in wondrous ways, founded upon exquisite wisdoms whose understanding bewilders minds and which none encompasses except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and who observes in the horizons the transformation of the darkness of night, which resembles death, into the light of day, which resembles life, and witnesses within himself the transformation of sleep, which is the brother of death, into waking, which is like life, judges that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah raises those who are in the graves, a firm decree; and is certain that He, exalted is He, has made this a model for it and a proof by which its realization may be inferred, and that the verses that declare it, and the state of night and day as a demonstration of it, and all the other signs, are a truth sent down from the presence of Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 87:

﴿And on the Day when the Trumpet is blown﴾ It is either coordinated with "the Day when We gather" (yawma nahshuru), in the accusative by its governing verb, or it is coordinated with an implied verb governed in the same way. The Trumpet (al-Sur) is the horn into which Israfil (peace be upon him) blows. It is related from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah the Exalted finished creating the heavens and the earth, He created the Trumpet and gave it to Israfil. He is holding it to his mouth, his gaze fixed on the Throne, waiting for when he will be commanded." He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what is the Trumpet?" He said, "The horn." I said, "What is it like?" He said, "It is great. By Him in whose hand my soul is, the circumference of its opening is as wide as the heavens and the earth. He will be commanded to blow into it, and he will blow a blast after which no one alive will remain except whomever Allah the Exalted wills. This is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom Allah wills﴾. Then he will be commanded to blow another, and he will blow a blast after which no dead person will remain except that he is raised and stands up. This is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on﴾." What the coherence and context of the noble arrangement require is that the blowing intended here is the second blast, and by the terror mentioned in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾ is meant the dread and awe, both of them natural and compelling, that overtake everyone at the Resurrection and the Gathering upon witnessing the tremendous matters that break the customary order, within souls and across horizons. The use of the past-tense form together with the fact that the preceding verb, "yunfakhu" (is blown), is in the present tense indicates the certainty of its occurrence immediately following the blast. Perhaps the delay in explaining the circumstances that occur at the onset of the blast, relative to explaining what follows it, namely the gathering of the deniers from every community, serves to double the awe through repeated reminder, signalling that each of these two is a supreme calamity and a terrible catastrophe worthy of being mentioned on its own. Had the chronological order of occurrence been observed, one might have imagined that the whole was a single calamity that had been commanded to be mentioned, as was the case in the story of the cow.

﴿Except whom Allah wills﴾ That is, that they should not be terrified. It has been said they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and Izra'il (peace be upon them). It has also been said they are the houris, the guardians, and the bearers of the Throne.

﴿And all﴾ That is, every one of those resurrected at the blast ﴿come to Him﴾: they attend the place of standing before the Lord of Might, may His majesty be exalted, for questioning, answering, discussion and reckoning. It is also read "atahu" (he came), taking into account the wording of "all," just as the first reading takes into account its meaning. It is also read "atuhu" (they are present before Him), meaning: present before Him.

﴿Humbled﴾ That is, abased. It is also read "dakhirin."

The verbal noun "wa-qawluhu" and the rest of the commentary follow.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you see the mountains﴾ is a conjunction with "yunfakhu" (﴿is blown﴾), falling under the same ruling of reminder. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿you think them solid﴾ means: firmly fixed in their places. It is either a substitute (badal) for it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "tara" (you see) or from its object.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿while they pass by as the clouds pass﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "al-jibal" (the mountains) in "tahsabuha" or in "jamidatan." That is: you see them, with your own eyes, as still, while in fact they pass as the clouds pass, which the winds drive with a swift motion. This is because great bodies, when they move in a direction, are hardly perceived to be moving. To this refers the saying of one who said:

*With a host as huge as a mountain, you think them*
*Standing still for pilgrims, while the mounts pace smoothly.*

This simile also incorporates the state of the mountains with the state of the clouds in the loosening and scattering of their parts, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the mountains will be like tufts of carded wool﴾. This too occurs after the second blast, at the gathering of creation. God, Mighty and Majestic, will change the earth into another earth, alter its form, and set the mountains moving from their places, in the terrifying shape mentioned, so that the people of the gathering may witness it. Although they will be crumbled and split at the first blast, their movement and the leveling of the earth will occur only after the second blast, as His saying, Exalted is He, expresses: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains; say: My Lord will scatter them with a scattering﴾ ﴿and will leave it a level plain﴾ ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or unevenness﴾ ﴿On that day they will follow the caller …﴾ And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed into another earth, and the heavens too, and they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer﴾. Indeed, following the caller, who is Israfil (peace be upon him), and the emergence of creation before God, Exalted is He, can occur only after the second blast.

Some have said, in explaining His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And on the day We set the mountains moving and you see the earth bare, and We gather them …﴾, that the past tense used in the conjoined clause, though the thing conjoined to is in the future, serves to indicate that the gathering precedes the moving and the seeing, as if it were said: "and We had gathered them before that."

That said, it has also been said that the intended meaning is the first blast, and that the "fazaʿ" (terror) is that which brings death, owing to the extreme intensity of the dread, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is in the earth will swoon …﴾ (the verse). Its effect is then restricted to those who were alive at its occurrence, excluding those of earlier nations who had died before it. It has also been allowed that by "coming" (al-ityan) in "dakhirin" is meant their return to His command and their submission to Him. Yet there is no doubt that this is something the sanctity of the revelation should be spared from. Further removed from this is what has been said: that the intended blast here is the blast of terror (nafkhat al-fazaʿ) which occurs before the blast of swooning, which is the one meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And these wait for nothing but one cry, with no respite﴾. Then God, Exalted is He, will set the mountains moving at that moment, so they pass as the clouds pass and become a mirage, and the earth will be shaken with its inhabitants with a violent shaking, becoming like a ship moored in the sea, or like a hanging lamp swayed by the winds. (p-305) This is clearly unconnected to the context. The truth from which there is no escape is what we have already set forth. And among what is explicit on this matter is His saying, Exalted is He, to come: ﴿And they will be secure from terror on that day﴾.
