﴿Ṣun'a Allah﴾ (the making of God) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of what precedes it: God has made that a making, meaning that the blowing into the Trumpet and all that follows from it is referred to together, and it is intended to draw attention to the great importance of those acts and the awesomeness of their matter, and to announce that they are not a way of disrupting the order of the world or corrupting the conditions of beings entirely, without any cause calling for it or any consequence for it. Rather, they belong to the wondrous works of God, Exalted is He, founded on wisdom that leads to the beautiful ends for which the preliminaries of creation and the beginnings of origination were arranged in a firm manner and a sound pattern. This is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who perfected everything﴾, that is, He made its creation firm and set it in order according to what wisdom requires.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed He is Aware of what you do﴾ is a causal explanation (taʿlil) for why what was mentioned is a firmly made work of His, Exalted is He, by showing that His knowledge, Exalted is He, of the outward and inward acts of the responsible persons is something that calls for their manifestation and for the explanation of their modes as they are, in goodness and evil. The ordering of their recompense upon them after their resurrection and gathering, and the arrangement of the heavens, the earth and the mountains in accordance with what the revelation has stated, is so that they may, by witnessing it, be certain that God's promise is true, without doubt. It has also been read: "Aware of what they do."

And His saying, ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him there is better than it﴾, is an explanation of what was alluded to by His, exalted is He, comprehensive knowledge of their deeds, namely the arrangement of their recompenses for them. That is: whoever among you, or among those who came to Him, exalted is He, with a good deed, for him there is a reward that is better than it, either in terms of its being multiplied many times over, or in terms of its lasting and not ending. It was also said: "for him there is a good that comes from it, which is Paradise." And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the good deed is the word of testimony (kalimat al-shahadah).

﴿And they﴾, that is, those who came with the good deeds, are ﴿safe from terror﴾, that is, a great, overwhelming terror whose extent cannot be measured, which is the terror that arises from witnessing the punishment after the reckoning is complete and the good and bad deeds have become manifest. This is the terror referred to in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them ...﴾. It is related from al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him): it is when the servant is ordered to the Fire. Ibn Jurayj said: it is when death is slaughtered, and the caller calls out: "O people of Paradise, eternity, there is no death! O people of the Fire, eternity, there is no death!"

﴿On that day﴾, that is, the day when the Trumpet is blown, they are ﴿secure﴾, not affected by that overwhelming terror, and no harm from it reaches them at all. As for the terror that affects everyone in the heavens and on the earth, except those whom Allah, exalted is He, excepts, it is merely the awe and dread that arise at the beginning of the blast from beholding the various calamities and terrors. Hardly anyone is free of it by the disposition of human nature, even if he is safe from harm reaching him. The verb "amina" (to be secure) is used with a preposition and without one, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah ...﴾.

It was also recited as "min faz'in yawma'idhin" (from a terror on that day) with an idafah (genitive construction), with the mim both kasrah and fathah. The intended meaning is the terror mentioned in the first recitation, not all the terrors that occur on that day. The basis of the idafah is that it is the greatest and most severe of the terrors, as if whatever else there is in comparison to it is not a terror at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 90:

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and they will be safe from the terror of that Day.﴾ — wait, that is not the verse under discussion. Let me give the translation of the passage as it stands:

﴿And whoever comes with the evil deed﴾ — it has been said: it is shirk (associating partners with God). ﴿Their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾ — i.e., they will be thrown into it face-down, upside down. Or: their selves will be overturned in it, following the manner of His saying: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [2:195].

﴿Are you being recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ — this is in the manner of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person) for emphasis (tashdid), or by supposing an implied speech (idmar al-qawl); i.e., it is said to them: that.

(p-306)﴿Indeed, I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. He (ﷺ) was commanded to say this to them after he had explained to them the circumstances of the origin (*mabda'*) and the return (*ma'ad*), and had described the circumstances of the Resurrection. This was to alert them that he had completed the matter of the call (*da'wah*) in a way that left nothing to add, and that after this he (ﷺ) had no concern except occupying himself with the worship of God, Mighty and Majestic, and being absorbed in watching over Him, indifferent to them, whether they went astray or were guided, whether they reformed or corrupted. This was so that it would move them to attend to the affairs of their own souls, and so that they would not imagine, because of the intensity of his (ﷺ) care for the matter of their call, that he (ﷺ) would display to them what would compel them to faith inevitably, and so that they would busy themselves with amending their conditions and turn toward reflecting on the dazzling signs they had witnessed. "The city" is Makkah the Honored. Its specification by the construct phrase serves to magnify its status, to exalt its place, and to draw attention to God's sanctifying it, which is an honour upon an honour and a glorification following a glorification. It also indicates the reason for the command and the obligation to comply with it, as in God's words: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾. It also points, by allusion, to the extreme enormity of what they did in it: even though it is sacred, such that its sanctity must not be violated, they nonetheless violated it by felling its trees, cutting its plants, frightening its game, and intending wrongdoing in it in any manner. They persisted in it in committing the most profligate of wicked deeds and the most abominable of acts of impiety, in that they abandoned the worship of its Lord, set up idols in it, and devoted themselves to worshipping them: ﴿May God destroy them; how are they deluded?﴾ It has been read as "*ḥaramahā*" with the lighter form (without the doubling of the *rā'*).

God's words ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ mean: in creation, sovereignty, and disposal, without anything sharing with Him in any part of that. This establishes the truth and alerts that singling out Makkah by the construct phrase for the aforementioned magnification and honour does not contradict the generality of Lordship over all existing things.

﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾ means: I remain steadfast in what I have been upon, being among those who are firmly established upon the religion of Islam and tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), that is, those who submitted their faces wholly to God, from God's words: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God?﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 27, verse 92:

﴿And that I should recite the Qur'an.﴾ That is: that I should persevere in its recitation, so that its wondrous truths, stored within its folds, may be unveiled to me little by little; or [that I should persevere] in reciting it to the people, by way of repeating the call and reiterating guidance, and this would be a warning of its sufficiency for guidance and direction without any need for the manifestation of another miracle. Thus the meaning of His exalted words: ﴿Whoever is guided, is only guided for [the benefit of] his own soul﴾ — then, whoever is guided by believing in it and acting upon the laws and rulings it contains; and according to the first [interpretation]: whoever is guided by following me in what has been mentioned of worship, submission, and the recitation of the Qur'an, then the benefits of his guidance return only to him, not to me.

﴿And whoever goes astray﴾ by disbelieving in it and turning away from acting upon what is in it, or by opposing me in what has been mentioned.

﴿Then say﴾ concerning him: ﴿I am only one of the warners.﴾ I have discharged the obligation of warning, so there is nothing upon me from the burden of his misguidance; rather, it is upon him alone.

(p-307) ﴿Say: "Praise be to God."﴾ That is, for the blessings He has bestowed upon me, the greatest of which is the blessing of prophethood, which brings with it all kinds of religious and worldly blessings, and for enabling me to bear its burdens and to convey its rulings to all people with clear signs and luminous proofs.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He will show you His signs﴾ is part of the speech that is commanded [to be said]; that is: He will surely show you in this world His manifest signs that the Qur'an has spoken of, such as the emergence of the beast (al-dabba) and the rest of the portents (al-ashrat). Among them is counted the Battle of Badr. The following words of His, exalted is He, ﴿and you will recognize them﴾, which is to say, you will recognize that they are the signs of God, exalted is He, at a time when recognition will not benefit you, argue against this, because they do not acknowledge that the Battle of Badr was such [a sign]. It has also been said: He will show [them] to you in the Hereafter.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a statement issued from Him, exalted is He, by way of a concluding affirmation (tadhyil), confirming what precedes it and containing both promise and threat, as is indicated by the attribution of the Lord to the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ, and by the address being first specified to him (ﷺ) and then generalized to the disbelievers by way of prevalence (taghlib). That is: "Your Lord is not unaware of what you (O Prophet) do of good deeds, nor of what you (disbelievers) do of evil deeds," so He will surely recompense each of you for his deeds without fail. It is also read: "what they do" (ya'malūn) in the third person, in which case it is a pure threat, and the meaning is: "Your Lord is not unaware of their deeds, so He will surely punish them; so let them not suppose that the delay of their punishment is due to God's unawareness of their deeds, which necessitate it." And God, exalted is He, knows best.

From the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever recites the Surah of Ta-Sin (Ṭā-Sīn), he will have a reward of ten good deeds for each person who believed in Solomon, Hud, Salih, Abraham and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, and for each who denied them, and he will come out of his grave while calling out: 'There is no god but God.'"
